lessons.title: Voltage, current and Ohm’s law
lessons.summary: Voltage is measured between two points; current passes through a component.
lessons.body:
Every circuit in a synth, from an LED on the front panel to the board's audio output, obeys a few simple rules. Learn them well now and the rest of this module is mostly applying them.

> [!warning] Low voltage only
> This module covers low-voltage DC work only: USB power, bench supplies of a few volts, and batteries. It does **not** cover mains wiring or mains power supplies. Use a ready-made, certified supply (a USB charger or a bench supply) and never open or modify anything that plugs into the wall.

## Four quantities
**Voltage** (written V, measured in volts, also V) is the difference in electrical potential between two points. It is the "push". A voltage is always *between* two points. "This pin is at 3.3 V" really means "3.3 V higher than ground".

**Electric current** (written I, measured in amperes or amps, A) is the rate at which charge flows past a point. One amp is one coulomb per second. Current flows *through* things.

**Electrical resistance** (written R, measured in ohms, Ω) is how strongly something opposes current. A resistor is a part made to have a known resistance.

**Electrical power** (written P, measured in watts, W) is the rate at which energy is transferred, for example turned into heat in a resistor or into light in an LED.

## Ohm's law
Ohm's law is the rule you use most: it links the voltage across a resistor to the current through it. For an ohmic resistor at roughly constant temperature, the two are proportional. Double the voltage and the current doubles. The resistance is the fixed ratio between them:

```formula essential
I = V / R
where
I: current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
V: voltage across the resistor, in volts (V)
R: resistance, in ohms (Ω)
In words: For an ohmic resistor at a fixed temperature, more voltage drives more current; more resistance allows less current at the same voltage.
```

With 5 V across 1 kΩ, the current is 5 mA. Doubling the voltage doubles that current if the resistance stays fixed; doubling the resistance instead halves it.

Ohm's law models ohmic resistors and the resistive part of wires when temperature and other conditions keep their resistance effectively fixed. It does not describe LEDs and diodes. Their current rises steeply with forward voltage rather than following a fixed resistance. Dividing voltage by current describes an operating point; it does not give a constant resistance that predicts another point. Apply Ohm’s law to the resistor in series with the LED, as in the neighbouring LED units.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Pressure and flow
> A pump can create a pressure difference even when a valve prevents flow.
>
> **How it maps:** Voltage is like pressure difference, current like flow rate, and a resistor like a restriction. A larger restriction passes less flow under the same pressure.
>
> **Where it stops:** This compares steady behaviour only. Charge, electric fields, energy storage and changing signals need the electrical explanation; voltage is always measured between two points.

## Key takeaways

- Voltage is measured between two points; current passes through a component.
- Use Ohm’s law for resistors at the stated operating conditions, not for LEDs.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: Ohm’s law](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-4-ohms-law)
- [OpenStax: electric current](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-1-electrical-current)

questions.prompt: You replace a resistor with one of twice the resistance, keeping the same DC voltage across it. Assume both are ohmic and stay at the same temperature. What happens to current?

options.text: It doubles
options.explanation: More resistance allows less current at a fixed voltage, not more.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: Holding voltage fixed does not hold current fixed; the resistance sets the relationship.

options.text: It becomes zero
options.explanation: A larger finite resistance reduces current without opening the circuit.

options.text: It halves
options.explanation: Correct. The same voltage drives half the current through twice the resistance.

questions.workedExample: First identify what stays fixed: voltage and temperature. Increasing resistance makes the path less conductive. Twice the resistance therefore halves the current. This prediction concerns an ohmic resistor, not an LED treated as a fixed resistor.

questions.prompt: Two unknown ohmic resistors have the same steady voltage across them. One carries less current. What does that tell you?

options.text: It must have the smaller resistance
options.explanation: At the same voltage, a smaller resistance would pass more current.

options.text: Its resistance cannot be compared without memorising a formula
options.explanation: The relationship is enough: resistance opposes current for a given voltage.

options.text: It has the larger resistance
options.explanation: Correct. Less current at the same voltage means greater resistance.

options.text: It must be an open circuit
options.explanation: A finite smaller current does not imply a broken path.

questions.workedExample: Compare the parts under the same voltage and temperature conditions. The part passing less current opposes that flow more strongly, so it has more resistance. An actual component value would require a measurement and calculation, but the comparison does not.

lessons.title: Resistor heat and an LED power budget
lessons.summary: Check resistor heat as well as current.
lessons.body:
A resistor can have the right resistance and still overheat. Check how much electrical energy it turns into heat each second, then compare that power with the part’s rating under the actual mounting and temperature conditions.

## Current alone does not tell you the heat
For a two-terminal part, power depends on both the voltage across it and the current through it:

```formula essential
P = VI
where
P: instantaneous absorbed power, in watts (W)
V: voltage across the part, in volts (V), using the labelled positive terminal
I: current entering that positive terminal, in amperes (A)
In words: Voltage times current gives the rate of energy transfer. Positive absorbed power means the part receives energy; negative means it supplies energy.
```

For steady DC this also gives average power. With changing signals, average the instantaneous product; multiplying arbitrary RMS voltages and currents is not a universal power rule. A chip with multiple terminals may need several power paths included.

For a fixed ohmic resistor, doubling the voltage also doubles the current, so it produces four times as much heat. At fixed voltage, increasing resistance reduces current and heat. At fixed current, increasing resistance requires more voltage and increases heat. Always say what stays fixed.

```formula reference
P = I^2 R
P = V^2 / R
where
P: resistor heat dissipation, in watts (W)
I: current through the resistor, in amperes (A)
R: the fixed resistance, in ohms (Ω)
V: voltage across the resistor, in volts (V)
In words: For a fixed resistor, heat rises with the square of voltage or current. These alternative forms use Ohm’s law and do not model an LED as a fixed resistor.
```

## Leave a thermal margin
An illustrative 100 Ω resistor directly across 5 V dissipates 0.25 W. A part rated for 0.25 W would be at its stated limit only under the specified thermal conditions; it need not feel cool. Choose a suitable higher-rated part, or reduce current if the circuit permits. Check the manufacturer’s derating curve, ambient temperature and mounting rather than treating a fixed safety factor as universal.

An LED and its resistor share the supply voltage. If a 330 Ω resistor carries a measured steady 10 mA from a 5 V supply, it drops 3.3 V and dissipates 33 mW; the LED has the remaining 1.7 V. That is an illustrative budget, not a claim about an arbitrary LED’s forward voltage. The resistor and LED carry the same series current, but their different voltage drops mean different powers.

## Key takeaways

- Resistance and wattage answer different questions: current control and allowed heat.
- Check voltage and current together, then the real part’s thermal conditions.
- Low voltage does not prevent a low-resistance path from overheating.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: electrical energy and power](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-5-electrical-energy-and-power)
- [SparkFun: LED current limiting](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/light-emitting-diodes-leds/all)
- [Vishay MRS16/MRS25: thermal conditions and derating](https://www.vishay.com/docs/28724/mrs16m25.pdf)

questions.prompt: A circuit calculation says a resistor will dissipate 0.25 W continuously. Its datasheet permits 0.25 W only under specified thermal conditions. What should you do before fitting it?

options.text: Ignore the rating because the supply is only 5 V
options.explanation: Low voltage can still create substantial heat in a low-resistance path.

options.text: Check actual temperature and mounting, and choose suitable thermal margin
options.explanation: Correct. Dissipation ratings depend on conditions; operating at the label value need not be cool or appropriate.

options.text: Assume it must fail immediately at exactly 0.25 W
options.explanation: A rating is not a prediction of instantaneous failure. Conditions and duration matter.

options.text: Change only to a tighter resistance tolerance
options.explanation: Tolerance may affect the calculated heat, but does not replace a wattage and derating check.

questions.workedExample: The heat calculation and the permitted dissipation are separate facts. Compare them at the real ambient temperature and mounting arrangement using the derating curve. Choose a suitable higher-rated part or reduce dissipation if the circuit permits, then check the changed design.

questions.prompt: Which statements about power in resistors are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor quadruples its power
options.explanation: Correct. With resistance fixed, power is proportional to voltage squared. Doubling voltage therefore gives four times the heat.

options.text: For a fixed current, a larger resistor dissipates more power
options.explanation: Correct. At fixed current, resistor heat increases in proportion to resistance.

options.text: For a fixed voltage, a larger resistor dissipates more power
options.explanation: At fixed voltage, increasing resistance reduces current and dissipated power. What stays fixed matters.

options.text: The voltage-times-current power rule applies only to resistors
options.explanation: Instantaneous voltage times current gives absorbed power for a two-terminal part under the passive sign convention. The squared resistor formulas additionally require Ohm’s law.

questions.workedExample: With resistance fixed, doubling voltage doubles current as well, so heat increases fourfold. If current instead stays fixed, a larger resistor needs more voltage and dissipates more power. If voltage stays fixed, a larger resistor passes less current and dissipates less. The voltage-times-current rule applies to any two-terminal part with the stated sign convention; the squared resistor forms additionally assume Ohm’s law.

lessons.title: Reading electronic units and prefixes
lessons.summary: Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.
lessons.body:
Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.

## Units and prefixes
Electronics spans huge ranges, so SI prefixes are everywhere. A prefix mistake can change a part by orders of magnitude.

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor |
|---|---|---|
| mega | M | 10⁶ |
| kilo | k | 10³ |
| milli | m | 10⁻³ |
| micro | µ (or u) | 10⁻⁶ |
| nano | n | 10⁻⁹ |
| pico | p | 10⁻¹² |

Tips:

- Note the case: **m** (milli) and **M** (mega) differ by 10⁹.
- Schematics often put the prefix where the decimal point would be (the RKM code, part of IEC 60062): `4k7` means 4.7 kΩ, `2R2` means 2.2 Ω, and `100n` means 100 nF.
- Match the value and unit when comparing a schematic with a parts list. `100n`, 100 nF and 0.1 µF describe the same capacitance; 100 µF is a thousand times larger.

Matching capacitance alone does not establish an interchangeable part. Also check its voltage rating (allowed voltage), dielectric (insulating material) and tolerance (allowed value variation), as specified for the circuit.

## Key takeaways

- Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.
- Check prefixes before fitting a part; a familiar-looking number may represent a very different value.

## Further reading

- [BIPM: SI prefixes](https://www.bipm.org/en/measurement-units/si-prefixes)
- [Vishay: resistor colour code](https://www.vishay.com/docs/49411/resistor_color_code_calculator.pdf)

questions.prompt: The schematic requires a 100 nF capacitor. Your parts list gives 0.1 µF; a prefix chart says one microfarad is one thousand nanofarads. What is the sensible next step?

options.text: Treat the capacitances as equal, then check voltage rating, dielectric and tolerance
options.explanation: Correct. The prefixes express the same nominal capacitance, but value alone does not establish a suitable replacement.

options.text: Reject it because different prefixes always mean different parts
options.explanation: Different units can express the same physical value.

options.text: Fit a 100 µF part because the number 100 matches
options.explanation: That ignores the prefix and selects a capacitance one thousand times larger.

options.text: Assume every 0.1 µF part is interchangeable
options.explanation: Equal capacitance does not guarantee suitable voltage rating or other characteristics.

questions.workedExample: Read the unit as part of the value. One tenth of a thousand nanofarads is 100 nF, so the nominal capacitance matches. Then check the properties the value marking does not establish. The prefix chart is a lookup aid, not something you must memorise.

lessons.title: Complete loops and LED current
lessons.summary: A steady current needs a complete current return path.
lessons.body:
A steady current needs a complete current return path.

## Complete circuits
In the steady low-voltage DC model, sustained conduction current flows around a **closed electrical loop** (a complete circuit): from the supply's positive terminal, through the load, and back to the supply's negative terminal. Break the loop anywhere (an open switch, a loose jumper, a cracked solder joint) and the current everywhere in that loop drops to zero.

```diagram
 +5V ---[ R 330 ]---[ LED >| ]---+
  |                              |
 supply                          |
  |                              |
 0V -----------------------------+
          return path (ground)
```

Two consequences:

- **The current return path is part of the circuit.** A signal that leaves your synth board on one wire must come back on another. In ordinary unbalanced audio wiring, the sleeve or shield is that return; balanced audio uses a pair of signal conductors.
- **Current is the same everywhere in a single loop.** If 10 mA flows through the resistor, 10 mA flows through the LED. This is Kirchhoff's current law in its simplest form.

Kirchhoff's voltage law is the other half: around any closed loop, the voltage rises equal the drops. It's how you work out what is left for the LED once the resistor has taken its share.

For example, a steady 5 V supply with 3.3 V across the resistor leaves 1.7 V across the LED. Voltage is shared; current is not used up by the first component.

In this lumped, steady-DC model, include any significant wire resistance as another component. Kirchhoff’s laws do not require zero wire resistance. At high frequencies or with changing magnetic flux, the simple lumped model needs additional care.

A bare LED connected to a voltage source has no dependable current control: its current rises steeply with forward voltage. Use a suitable series resistor or specified current driver, and respect both the LED and any GPIO pin’s current limits.

## Conventional current and electron flow
Circuit diagrams and textbooks use **conventional current**: current flows from + to −. That convention predates the discovery of the electron. In a metal wire the charge carriers are actually electrons, which are negative and drift the opposite way, from − to +.

Both descriptions predict the same voltages, currents and power. Every formula, datasheet and schematic symbol uses conventional current. A forward-biased diode carries conventional current from anode to cathode (the bar). An LED's outward arrows indicate light, not current. Use conventional current and treat electron flow as a physics detail.

## Key takeaways

- A steady current needs a complete current return path.
- Use conventional current from anode to cathode through a forward-biased LED.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: Kirchhoff’s rules](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-3-kirchhoffs-rules)
- [OpenStax: electric current](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-1-electrical-current)
- [SparkFun: LED current limiting](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/light-emitting-diodes-leds/all)

questions.prompt: For a battery driving a forward-biased LED through a resistor, which statement about conventional current and the LED symbol is correct?

options.text: From − to +, because the arrow follows the electrons
options.explanation: Electrons in a wire do drift from − to +, but schematics and formulas use conventional current, which goes the other way.

options.text: Conventional current flows through the load from + to − and through the LED from anode to cathode; its outward arrows show light
options.explanation: Correct. The cathode is marked by the bar; LED emission arrows describe light.

options.text: It doesn't matter, because AC and DC circuits use opposite conventions
options.explanation: The convention is the same for AC and DC. In AC the direction alternates, but the reference direction is still defined using conventional current.

options.text: The LED's outward arrows show electron flow
options.explanation: Those arrows show light emission. Electrons in metal move opposite conventional current.

questions.workedExample:
1. Conventional current is defined in the direction of positive-charge flow: through the external load from battery + to −.
2. In the forward-biased LED it flows from anode to cathode (the bar).
3. The LED symbol's small outward arrows represent emitted light. They are not current arrows.

questions.prompt: A supply drives an LED and resistor in one series loop. A builder uses the entire supply voltage when estimating resistor current, ignoring the LED’s forward voltage. What is wrong?

options.text: The resistor and LED carry different currents
options.explanation: In this single series path they carry the same current.

options.text: The LED uses up the current before it reaches ground
options.explanation: Components share voltage drops, not a supply of current that gets consumed.

options.text: Ohm’s law cannot be used anywhere in a circuit containing an LED
options.explanation: It still applies to the ohmic resistor, using the voltage across that resistor.

options.text: The supply voltage is shared, so the resistor has only the voltage remaining after the LED drop
options.explanation: Correct. Ignoring the LED’s drop overestimates resistor current under the assumed forward-voltage model.

questions.workedExample: Trace one current path. The resistor and LED carry the same current, but the supply voltage is divided between them. Estimate the LED’s forward voltage at the intended current, then use the voltage remaining across the resistor. Real forward voltage changes with device, current and temperature.

questions.prompt: Your LED circuit, fed from a 3.3 V supply through a resistor, works on the breadboard. You unplug the jumper that connects the LED's cathode back to ground. What is the current through the resistor now?

options.text: Zero, because the loop is broken
options.explanation: Correct. Current only flows around a complete loop. Breaking it anywhere, even on the ground side, stops current everywhere in that loop.

options.text: Unchanged, because the resistor is still connected to +3.3 V
options.explanation: Being connected to the supply at one end isn't enough. Without a current return path no charge can flow.

options.text: Higher, because the LED is no longer dropping voltage
options.explanation: Opening the loop stops steady current, so the resistor has no voltage drop. A voltage can still exist across the open gap or other nodes; removing the return does not bypass the LED.

options.text: Half, because only one side of the circuit is connected
options.explanation: Current isn't shared out by how many ends are connected. A loop is either complete or it isn't.

questions.workedExample:
1. Trace the loop: + → resistor → LED → jumper → ground → back to the supply.
2. Remove the jumper and the loop is open.
3. With an open loop, the current is zero everywhere in it.
4. A consequence: with no current, there's no voltage drop across the resistor, so both its ends and the LED's anode now sit at 3.3 V. A meter shows 3.3 V at the LED's anode, which can confuse you when debugging.

questions.prompt: A beginner connects an LED straight from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin to ground, with no resistor, reasoning that "3.3 V is low, so it's safe". Why is this a bad idea?

options.text: LED current rises steeply with forward voltage, so the uncontrolled current can exceed the pin or LED rating
options.explanation: Correct. The quoted forward voltage is a test point, not a current regulator or fixed switching threshold. A suitable resistor or current driver sets the current.

options.text: LEDs need at least 5 V, so it simply won't light
options.explanation: Many LEDs, red ones especially, light well below 3.3 V. The risk isn't failure to light but too much current.

options.text: It's fine as long as the LED is red
options.explanation: Colour changes the forward voltage, but every LED has a steep current-voltage curve. Without a resistor the current is still uncontrolled.

options.text: The LED will reverse-bias and block all current
options.explanation: Connected anode to pin and cathode to ground, the LED is forward biased. Reverse bias is the wrong way round and is a different problem.

questions.workedExample: An LED’s forward current rises steeply as voltage rises; its quoted forward voltage is not a built-in current limit. A direct GPIO connection relies on uncontrolled LED and driver behaviour and can exceed either part’s rating. Use a correctly sized series resistor or specified current driver, checking the pin’s loaded output, per-pin and total-current limits, the LED limits and resistor heat.

lessons.title: Ground references and return-wire voltage
lessons.summary: Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.
lessons.body:
Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.

## Ground is a reference
**Circuit ground** (GND, 0 V) is the point you choose to measure every other voltage against. In a battery- or USB-powered synth it's usually the supply's negative terminal. It doesn't have to connect to the earth in the soil.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Heights measured from sea level
> A hill's height is usually quoted above sea level, but you could measure it from the valley floor instead. The hill does not change; only the number you quote does.
>
> **How it maps:** Circuit ground is the chosen zero, like sea level. "This pin is at 3.3 V" is a difference between the pin and that reference. Two boards can only compare voltages meaningfully when they share a reference.
>
> **Where it stops:** A height datum is a fixed, agreed reference that nothing flows through. Real ground conductors carry current and can sit at slightly different voltages from point to point. Protective earth is also a separate safety connection, not just a choice of zero.

Three meanings of "ground" get mixed up:

- **Signal or circuit ground:** the 0 V reference and current return path inside your circuit. This is what "GND" on a microcontroller board means.
- **Chassis ground:** the conductive case or chassis reference; whether it connects to circuit 0 V depends on the equipment design.
- **Protective earth:** the mains safety earth in a wall socket. It belongs to mains equipment and is not something to modify. The later noise and grounding units return to this.

Two practical rules follow:

1. **Direct, non-isolated single-ended signals need a common voltage reference.** For ordinary GPIO/UART links, connect the boards' GND pins. Isolated links such as DIN MIDI deliberately avoid a direct ground connection. A voltage only means something relative to a reference both sides agree on.
2. **"0 V" isn't the same everywhere.** Ground wires have small resistances. When current flows through them, two "ground" points can differ by a few millivolts. For audio that's enough to hear (the noise and grounding units).

## Key takeaways

- Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.
- Real return conductors develop voltage when current flows.

## Further reading

- [Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-031.pdf)
- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)

questions.prompt: Which statements about ground are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ground is the reference point other voltages are measured against
options.explanation: Correct. "This pin is at 3.3 V" means 3.3 V relative to ground.

options.text: Two boards connected by ordinary non-isolated single-ended GPIO signals need a shared ground reference
options.explanation: Correct for this connection. Isolated interfaces such as DIN MIDI deliberately do not join their circuit grounds.

options.text: Ground in a USB-powered circuit must be wired to the earth pin of a wall socket
options.explanation: Circuit ground is just the 0 V reference, usually the supply's negative terminal. Protective earth belongs to mains equipment, which you should leave alone.

options.text: Every ground point in a circuit is at exactly 0 V at all times
options.explanation: Ground conductors have resistance. Current through them produces small voltage differences between "ground" points, which matters for audio.

questions.workedExample: Ground is a chosen voltage reference. Ordinary direct single-ended GPIO links need a shared reference, while properly isolated interfaces avoid joining circuit grounds. Protective earth is a separate safety function and must remain intact. Real return conductors have resistance and inductance, so current can create voltage differences between points labelled ground.

questions.prompt: Board A sends a single-ended analogue signal to board B. Their grounds share a return wire carrying changing LED current. Why might B’s reading follow the LED pattern?

options.text: Ground labels force every point to remain at exactly the same voltage
options.explanation: A label identifies the intended reference; real conductors have impedance.

options.text: LEDs consume the signal’s voltage before it reaches B
options.explanation: The problem is a changing reference voltage in a shared conductor, not voltage being consumed upstream.

options.text: The changing return current creates a voltage drop between the boards’ references
options.explanation: Correct. B measures relative to its own ground, so a moving ground difference becomes a measurement error.

options.text: Any connection to ground automatically removes noise
options.explanation: A ground wire can carry the very current creating the disturbance.

questions.workedExample: Follow both signal and return paths. Current through the shared return wire creates a voltage difference between the references. If that current changes with the LEDs, the reference difference changes too. Separate sensitive references from noisy return currents according to the board’s grounding design.

lessons.title: Combining series and parallel resistors
lessons.summary: Series resistances add; parallel branches share a voltage.
lessons.body:
How resistors connect matters as much as their values. Trace which terminals share a connection before predicting the current.

## Series adds obstacles in one path
Components in a series circuit share one current path. The same current passes through each component; it is not used up along the way. Their voltage drops add to the supply voltage in this simple DC loop.

For resistors, series resistance adds. A 1 kΩ resistor followed by 2.2 kΩ behaves like 3.2 kΩ in the ideal model. Across the same supply, adding a positive series resistance reduces current.

## Parallel adds another path
Components in a parallel circuit connect across the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage. Each branch carries its own current, and those currents add at the supply. Adding a positive resistive branch increases total current from an ideal fixed-voltage supply; it does not reduce the voltage across the existing branch.

For positive finite resistors, the combined resistance is below the smallest branch. Two equal 10 kΩ resistors in parallel behave like 5 kΩ. A much larger parallel resistance has less effect: 1 MΩ across 10 kΩ gives about 9.9 kΩ because the added branch draws little extra current.

Conductance means how easily a path passes current: it is the reciprocal of resistance. Conductances add in parallel. For two resistors the useful calculation is:

```formula reference
R_total = (R1 R2) / (R1 + R2)
where
R_total: equivalent resistance of the parallel pair, in ohms (Ω)
R1: first positive branch resistance, in ohms
R2: second positive branch resistance, in ohms
In words: Two resistors connected across the same nodes provide more current paths, so their combined resistance is smaller than either one.
```

This reasoning assumes fixed, ohmic resistors and a supply that holds its voltage. A real supply can sag or enter current limit if the added branch demands too much current.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: One doorway or another route
> People moving through two narrow doorways in a row face both restrictions. Opening a separate route lets more people pass overall.
>
> **How it maps:** Series resistors put restrictions along one path; a parallel branch provides an additional path for current.
>
> **Where it stops:** People can wait and choose routes. In this steady electrical model, branch currents follow the applied voltage and resistance, and charge does not accumulate at a junction.

## Key takeaways

- Series parts share current; parallel parts share voltage.
- An extra series resistor reduces current from a fixed supply; an extra parallel branch increases total current.
- Use the connection pattern to sanity-check a calculated resistance.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: series and parallel resistors](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-2-resistors-in-series-and-parallel)

questions.prompt: Across an ideal fixed-voltage supply, you first add a second positive resistor in series with an existing resistor, then try it as a parallel branch instead. How does total supply current change?

options.text: Series reduces it; adding a parallel branch increases it
options.explanation: Correct. Series adds resistance to one path; parallel adds another path drawing current.

options.text: Series increases it; parallel reduces it
options.explanation: This reverses the effect of an added restriction versus an added path.

options.text: Both arrangements reduce current
options.explanation: A parallel branch adds supply current while the original branch keeps the same voltage.

options.text: Both arrangements leave current unchanged
options.explanation: A fixed supply voltage does not imply a fixed total current.

questions.workedExample: In series every charge path includes both resistors, so the equivalent resistance rises and current falls. In parallel the original resistor still has the same voltage, while the new branch draws additional current. The prediction assumes the supply holds its voltage rather than sagging or entering current limit.

lessons.title: Understanding an unloaded voltage divider
lessons.summary: The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input.
lessons.body:
A voltage divider uses two series resistors to make a fraction of a supply voltage. It is useful for a signal or reference feeding an input that draws very little current.

```diagram
 Vin ──┐
       R1
       ├──── Vout
       R2
 GND ──┘
```

## The lower resistor sets the output’s share
The same current flows through both resistors when the output is unloaded. The larger resistor therefore has the larger voltage drop. The output is measured from the junction to ground, so it is the voltage across the lower resistor.

Equal resistors divide the supply in half: two 10 kΩ parts across 3.3 V give 1.65 V unloaded. Making the upper resistor larger moves the junction towards ground; making the lower resistor larger moves it towards the supply.

```formula reference
Vout = Vin R2 / (R1 + R2)
where
Vout: unloaded junction voltage relative to ground, in volts (V)
Vin: voltage across the whole divider, in volts
R1: upper resistor from the supply to the junction, in ohms (Ω)
R2: lower resistor from the junction to ground, in ohms
In words: The output is the supply voltage multiplied by the lower resistor’s share of the total resistance. This assumes no current is drawn from the junction.
```

## Same ratio, different ability to drive a load
A pair of 1 kΩ resistors and a pair of 100 kΩ resistors both halve the voltage when unloaded. The smaller pair draws more continuous current from the supply but is less disturbed by a load. The larger pair wastes less power but its voltage is easier to pull down.

The ratio alone cannot tell you whether a real circuit will work. The next lesson adds the load; do not use an unloaded divider calculation as proof that it can power another board.

## Key takeaways

- The output is the lower resistor’s share of the supply.
- Changing both resistances by the same factor preserves the unloaded ratio.
- Resistance scale still determines current consumption and loading error.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)
- [OpenStax: series and parallel resistors](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-2-resistors-in-series-and-parallel)

questions.prompt: An unloaded divider has equal upper and lower resistors across a fixed supply. You increase only the upper resistor. What happens to the junction voltage measured from ground?

options.text: It stays halfway because there are still two resistors
options.explanation: Half the voltage requires equal resistances, not merely two components.

options.text: It rises towards the supply
options.explanation: A larger upper resistor takes a larger share of the supply drop, leaving less across the lower resistor.

options.text: It falls towards ground
options.explanation: Correct. The lower resistor now represents a smaller share of total resistance.

options.text: It rises above the supply
options.explanation: This passive divider cannot create a voltage above its positive supply in the stated circuit.

questions.workedExample: The unloaded series current flows through both resistors. Raising the upper resistance makes it take more of the voltage drop. The junction voltage is the lower resistor’s drop, so it falls. Check which resistor is connected to ground before making the prediction.

lessons.title: Loading, source resistance and divider limits
lessons.summary: Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first.
lessons.body:
A divider voltage can look right on paper and fall when you connect the next circuit. The added circuit draws current: it becomes part of the circuit you must analyse.

## A load changes the divider
A resistive load connected from the divider output to ground sits in parallel with the lower resistor. That combination has less resistance, so the output moves towards ground. The unloaded resistor ratio no longer describes it.

For example, two 10 kΩ resistors across 3.3 V give 1.65 V unloaded. Adding a 10 kΩ load makes the lower pair equivalent to 5 kΩ and pulls the output down to 1.10 V. These are ideal resistive examples, not measurements of a particular board.

## Source resistance tells you how easily it moves
The divider’s output resistance describes it as an ideal voltage source with a resistance in series. For a divider driven by an ideal voltage supply, its upper and lower resistors appear in parallel when finding that output resistance. This is a circuit-analysis step, not an instruction to short a real supply.

```formula reference
R_out = (R1 R2) / (R1 + R2)
where
R_out: divider output resistance with an ideal independent voltage supply, in ohms (Ω)
R1: upper divider resistance, in ohms
R2: lower divider resistance, in ohms
In words: The divider has a finite source resistance. A load much larger than this resistance changes its voltage less; a comparable load causes substantial sag.
```

Two 10 kΩ resistors have 5 kΩ output resistance. A resistive load ten times the output resistance causes about 9.1% sag; one hundred times causes about 1% sag. Choose against your allowed error, not a universal ten-times rule.

Reducing both divider resistances keeps the unloaded voltage but reduces sag for the same load. The cost is more divider standing current and power consumption. Raising both values does the opposite.

## An ADC is not just a resistor
Many ADC inputs briefly connect a sampling capacitor. A high source resistance may not charge it to the new voltage within the ADC acquisition time. The error can have either sign, depending on the capacitor’s previous charge. Check the specific ADC’s source-impedance and sampling-time guidance; a DC meter reading alone cannot confirm correct sampling.

## A divider is not a regulated power supply
A board draws significant, varying current. A high-resistance divider cannot maintain its intended voltage under that load. A dummy resistor can illustrate the sag, but it does not predict a real board’s startup behaviour. Use an appropriately specified voltage regulator for power, checking input range, output current, heat and required capacitors.

## Key takeaways

- A resistive load to ground pulls the divider output down.
- Lower source resistance improves loading error at the cost of continuous current.
- Check ADC acquisition requirements and use a regulator for board power.

## Further reading

- [TI: linear-regulator fundamentals](https://www.ti.com/video/series/power-fundamentals-linear-regulator-fundamentals.html)
- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)
- [OpenStax: series and parallel resistors](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-2-resistors-in-series-and-parallel)
- [Microchip: ADC acquisition time](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/products/data-converters/adc-specs/acquisition-time/)

options.text: The load raises the supply voltage
options.explanation: A load to ground does not raise the ideal supply in this model.

options.text: The two original resistors have physically changed value
options.explanation: Their values can stay unchanged; the circuit’s effective lower resistance changes because a branch was added.

options.text: A divider output must always be half the supply
options.explanation: Only equal unloaded resistors give half, and loading changes that condition.

options.text: The input is in parallel with the lower resistor, reducing its effective resistance
options.explanation: Correct. That changes the division ratio and pulls the output towards ground.

questions.workedExample: Trace the load’s two terminals. They match the lower resistor’s terminals, so the load is a parallel branch. Parallel resistance is smaller, making the lower branch’s share of the supply smaller. The unloaded calculation no longer describes the circuit.

questions.prompt: Two dividers have the same unloaded ratio, but one uses much larger resistors. Both feed the same resistive load to ground. What does higher output resistance imply?

options.text: Less loading error because it draws less standing current
options.explanation: Lower standing current is a benefit, but it comes with a weaker source and greater loading error.

options.text: The load can pull the output further below its unloaded voltage
options.explanation: Correct. More source resistance causes more voltage loss for the same load relationship.

options.text: The output becomes an ideal voltage source
options.explanation: An ideal source has zero output resistance; increasing it moves away from that model.

options.text: The divider can deliver more power to a board
options.explanation: High resistance restricts available output current; a divider is not a regulated supply.

questions.workedExample: Output resistance describes how far the voltage moves when current is drawn. Raising both divider resistances preserves the unloaded ratio but increases output resistance. The same load then changes the voltage more, even though the divider itself wastes less standing current.

questions.prompt: You want to run a 3.3 V board from a 5 V USB supply, so you build a divider from 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ and feed its output into the board's 3.3 V power pin. What happens?

options.text: The voltage collapses well below 3.3 V as soon as the board draws current, and varies with its load. Use a regulator instead
options.explanation: Correct. A divider's output depends on the load. A board drawing, say, 100 mA through a 1 kΩ top resistor would need a 100 V drop, which is impossible, so the output falls nearly to zero.

options.text: It works: 5 V × 2/3 = 3.33 V
options.explanation: That's the unloaded voltage. The board draws tens to hundreds of milliamps, which is a very heavy, varying load in parallel with the 2 kΩ.

options.text: The voltage rises above 3.3 V and damages the board
options.explanation: A passive load reduces this divider’s nominal output; it does not regulate it. The unloaded output is about 3.33 V, so exact supply, tolerance and board limits still matter. Do not use it as a board power supply.

options.text: It works if you use 10 kΩ and 20 kΩ instead to save power
options.explanation: Higher resistances make the output *weaker*. With 10 kΩ on top, the board could draw only a fraction of a milliamp before the voltage collapses.

questions.workedExample: The unloaded voltage can look correct on a meter, but a board is a significant and changing load. Current through the upper resistor creates additional voltage drop, so the output cannot stay at the intended value. Increasing both resistors reduces available current further. Use a specified regulator and check its input headroom, output current, heat and capacitor requirements; a dummy-resistor model cannot predict a real board’s startup voltage.

questions.prompt: You need a divider reference feeding a high-resistance input. Several resistor pairs give the desired unloaded ratio. How should you choose their scale?

options.text: Use the smallest values possible regardless of current
options.explanation: Very low values waste supply current and heat; low source resistance is not the only goal.

options.text: Use the largest values possible regardless of loading
options.explanation: Very high values let even a high-resistance input pull the voltage away from its target.

options.text: Balance loading error against standing current using the actual input requirements
options.explanation: Correct. The ratio sets unloaded voltage; the scale sets source resistance and current consumption.

options.text: Every pair with the same ratio works equally well when loaded
options.explanation: The load interacts with the individual resistances, not just their ratio.

questions.workedExample: Start with the desired ratio. Compare the load with the divider’s output resistance and your allowed voltage error. Lower values improve loading but consume more current. If the input samples a capacitor, check the ADC acquisition time as well as its static resistance.

lessons.title: Wiring a potentiometer to an ADC
lessons.summary: Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.
lessons.body:
Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.

## The potentiometer: a divider with a moving tap
A **potentiometer** (pot) is a resistive track with a wiper that slides along it. It has three terminals: the two ends of the track and the wiper.

```diagram
  pin 1 ──/\/\/\/\/\/\── pin 3
              ↑
           pin 2 (wiper)
```

Wire one end to the supply, the other to ground, and the wiper is a divider output. The wiper divides the fixed end-to-end track into an upper and a lower resistance; turning the knob changes their split, not their total. Moving towards the supply end increases the lower share and raises the unloaded output; moving towards ground lowers it.

For an unloaded linear 10 kΩ pot across 3.3 V, a quarter-track setting leaves 2.5 kΩ below the wiper and gives about 0.83 V. This assumes the ground end is the bottom and the track is ideal.

For a microcontroller knob:

```diagram
 3.3V ── pin 3
        pot track ── pin 2 ── ADC pin
 GND ── pin 1
```

Points to watch:

- **Use the board's documented analogue supply for the pot, matching the ADC range.** Do not load an unbuffered VREF pin unless the documentation explicitly allows it. If the pot is fed from a different voltage, the ADC's full range won't match the knob's full range. Feeding it from a higher voltage could also exceed the input's maximum (the logic and datasheet units).
- **Swapping pins 1 and 3** reverses the direction of the knob. It's harmless and easily fixed in software.
- **Never wire the wiper straight to a supply rail.** At one extreme the wiper sits at the end connected to ground, and you'd short the supply through a few ohms of track.
- **The pot's resistance** trades divider standing current against source impedance. Values around 10 kΩ are a common choice for microcontroller knobs, but confirm against the ADC's source-impedance limit.

## Worst-case source resistance

The source resistance seen by an ADC is the two track segments in parallel, assuming a stiff supply. It is lowest near the ends and largest where the two segments have equal resistance: at mid-rotation for an ideal linear pot. The maximum is one quarter of the total track resistance: 25 kΩ for a 100 kΩ pot, or 2.5 kΩ for a 10 kΩ pot.

A high source resistance can prevent the ADC’s sampling capacitor settling in time. Use a lower-value pot, a documented longer ADC acquisition time or a suitable buffer/filter arrangement as the ADC manufacturer recommends. A capacitor alone is not a universal fix.

## Key takeaways

- Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.
- A pot’s wiper source resistance peaks in the middle of a linear track.

## Further reading

- [Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts](https://www.bourns.com/docs/product-datasheets/PDB181-GTR.pdf)
- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)
- [PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)
- [Microchip: ADC acquisition time](https://developerhelp.microchip.com/xwiki/bin/view/products/data-converters/adc-specs/acquisition-time/)

options.text: The total resistance between 3.3 V and ground
options.explanation: The track between the two ends is fixed. Only the wiper's position on it changes.

options.text: The ratio of the two parts of the track, and so the divider's output voltage
options.explanation: Correct. The wiper splits the fixed track into an upper part and a lower part. Their ratio sets the wiper voltage, from 0 V to 3.3 V.

options.text: The current drawn from the supply, from zero to maximum
options.explanation: The current through the track is 3.3 V divided by the pot's total resistance, which is constant whatever the wiper position (ignoring the ADC's tiny load).

options.text: The ADC's reference voltage
options.explanation: The reference is fixed by the board. The pot produces a voltage between 0 V and its top end, which the ADC measures against that reference.

questions.workedExample: The supply remains across the whole resistive track. Turning the knob moves the tap, increasing one segment while decreasing the other. Their ratio changes the wiper voltage while the end-to-end resistance stays fixed. This ideal explanation assumes negligible loading; real ADC acquisition current and source impedance still need checking.

options.text: The pot’s total resistance doubles in the middle

options.text: The ADC must be damaged because a pot is always a perfect voltage source
options.explanation: A pot has finite source resistance, which interacts with the ADC’s sampling capacitor.

options.text: The voltage exceeds the supply at mid-rotation

questions.prompt: Which statements about wiring a pot to a microcontroller are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Swapping the two end pins reverses the knob's direction but is otherwise harmless
options.explanation: Correct. It mirrors the divider, and you can invert it in software if you prefer.

options.text: Connecting the wiper directly to 3.3 V and one end to ground risks shorting the supply when the knob is at that end
options.explanation: Correct. At that extreme the wiper sits on the grounded end, connecting 3.3 V to ground through almost zero track resistance.

options.text: Feed the pot from the documented analogue supply matching the ADC range, with its wiper always within the input-voltage limits
options.explanation: Correct. Match the documented input range and supply limits. Do not load an unbuffered VREF pin unless its documentation permits it.

options.text: Feeding the pot from 5 V gives better resolution on a 3.3 V ADC
options.explanation: The ADC can't measure above its reference, and on 3.3 V-only pins 5 V can damage the chip. It loses part of the range and risks damage.

Wiring the wiper to a supply while an end is grounded can instead create a near-short at one extreme. Power the track from the documented analogue supply and keep every wiper position within the ADC input limits; do not assume a VREF output can supply the pot. A 5 V track can overdrive a 3.3 V-only input over part of its travel.

lessons.title: Linear and audio potentiometer tapers
lessons.summary: Taper describes resistance versus rotation.
lessons.body:
Taper describes resistance versus rotation.

## Linear and logarithmic (audio) taper
The **potentiometer taper** (or law) is how resistance changes with rotation.

- **Linear taper:** halfway round, the wiper is at half the total resistance. With negligible loading and a steady supply, output voltage is approximately proportional to angle over the usable track.
- **Logarithmic or "audio" taper:** the resistance changes slowly at first, then quickly. Audio tapers are often specified by the share of resistance at mid-rotation: a 10% taper puts the wiper at about 10% of the total there, and 15% versions also exist (Bourns PDB181-GTR offers both). Loudness perception is roughly logarithmic, so an audio taper makes an analogue volume control feel more even than a linear one.

| Rotation | Linear | 10% log (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | 0% | 0% |
| 50% | 50% | 10% |
| 100% | 100% | 100% |

Two practical warnings:

- **Markings aren't standardised.** For example, Bourns PDB181-GTR uses its A-series audio curves and B0 linear curve. Other manufacturers and legacy parts use different letter schemes. Read the datasheet.
- **Audio tapers follow specified curves.** They need not be exact mathematical logarithms; use the manufacturer’s curve for the actual part.

> [!tip] For digital synths, usually choose linear
> When a pot feeds an ADC, you can choose the response curve in software, within the available resolution. An ideal linear pot with negligible loading spreads ADC resolution roughly evenly across usable rotation, and code can map it to a logarithmic volume or exponential frequency response. A log pot is mostly useful when it directly controls an analogue audio level.

## Key takeaways

- Taper describes resistance versus rotation.
- Verify the manufacturer’s marking scheme rather than assuming a letter code.

## Further reading

- [Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts](https://www.bourns.com/docs/product-datasheets/PDB181-GTR.pdf)

questions.prompt: A pot marked "B10K" arrives from a supplier. What can you safely conclude?

options.text: It is 10 kΩ and certainly linear
options.explanation: "B" commonly means linear on Asian and US parts, but the letters aren't standardised. Some European makers use other letter schemes.

options.text: It is 10 kΩ log, because B stands for "bass"
options.explanation: There's no such convention. Taper codes vary by maker; "B" is often linear.

options.text: It is 10 kΩ, and the taper letter suggests linear on many parts but should be confirmed in the datasheet or by measuring
options.explanation: Correct. 10K is the track resistance. The taper letter convention varies between manufacturers, so check the datasheet, or measure the wiper resistance at mid-rotation (about 5 kΩ for linear, about 1 kΩ for a 10% log).

options.text: It is a 10 kΩ fixed resistor
options.explanation: "K" is the kilohm multiplier. The letter in front is the taper code of a potentiometer.

questions.workedExample:
1. "10K" gives the end-to-end track resistance: 10 kΩ.
2. The taper letter isn't standardised. A/B/C have different meanings between regions and makers.
3. Confirm: set the knob to mid-rotation and measure from one end to the wiper, with the pot out of circuit (unpowered).
   - About 5 kΩ means linear.
   - About 1 kΩ (or 9 kΩ from the other end) means a 10% log taper.

link.title: Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts

questions.prompt: Which of these are reasons to choose a *linear* pot for a knob read by a microcontroller ADC? Select all that apply.

options.text: You can apply any response curve in software after reading it
options.explanation: Correct. Code can map the reading to an exponential frequency or logarithmic level curve.

options.text: It spreads the ADC's resolution evenly across the rotation
options.explanation: Correct. With a log pot, much of the rotation is squeezed into a small part of the ADC range, wasting codes at one end.

options.text: Log pots can't be connected to ADCs
options.explanation: A log pot works electrically. It's just a divider with a track whose resistance share is not proportional to rotation. The point is that it's usually unnecessary.

options.text: Linear pots have lower noise than log pots in all cases
options.explanation: There's no general rule that taper decides noise. This isn't a reason taught in the lesson.

questions.workedExample:
1. The ADC converts voltage to a number. Any curve after that is arithmetic.
2. Linear pot: equal rotation gives equal ADC codes, so resolution is even everywhere.
3. 10% log pot: the first half of the rotation covers only 10% of the voltage range, so it gets about a tenth of the codes. That's coarse at the start.
4. Log pots are still useful when the pot directly sets an analogue audio level with no software in between.

lessons.title: Reading resistor colour bands
lessons.summary: Read digits, multiplier and tolerance separately.
lessons.body:
A synth build uses a small set of passive parts over and over. Each one has a **value** (what it does) and **ratings** (what it survives). Ignoring ratings or component polarity can damage parts even when the nominal value is correct.

## Reading the value
Through-hole resistors use colour bands defined by IEC 60062. Read from the end where the bands bunch together. The gold or silver tolerance band is usually at the other end, often slightly separated.

| Colour | Digit | Multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| Black | 0 | ×1 |
| Brown | 1 | ×10 |
| Red | 2 | ×100 |
| Orange | 3 | ×1k |
| Yellow | 4 | ×10k |
| Green | 5 | ×100k |
| Blue | 6 | ×1M |
| Violet | 7 | ×10M |
| Grey | 8 | ×100M |
| White | 9 | ×1G |
| Gold | | ×0.1 |
| Silver | | ×0.01 |

- **Four-band resistor code:** digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Yellow-violet-red-gold = 4, 7, ×100 = 4.7 kΩ ±5%.
- **Five-band resistor code** (precision): digit, digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Brown-black-black-red-brown = 1, 0, 0, ×100 = 10 kΩ ±1%.
- **Tolerance band:** brown ±1%, red ±2%, gold ±5%, silver ±10%.

The digit bands form a whole number, and the multiplier band scales it. For four bands, read the first two as a number, apply the multiplier from the chart, then check tolerance. Keep the chart nearby rather than memorising every colour.

A five-band resistor uses three significant digits. Brown-black-black-red-brown has three digits followed by the red multiplier and brown tolerance. For five bands, read three significant digits before the multiplier and tolerance. Counting the bands first prevents mistaking a multiplier for a digit.

Colours are easy to misread under poor light. Brown, red and orange look alike, and so do violet and grey. **Measure with a multimeter before fitting** (out of circuit) whenever you're unsure.

## Key takeaways

- Read digits, multiplier and tolerance separately.
- Confirm uncertain colours by measuring the unpowered resistor out of circuit.

## Further reading

- [Vishay: resistor colour code](https://www.vishay.com/docs/49411/resistor_color_code_calculator.pdf)

questions.prompt: A four-band resistor has yellow, violet, orange and gold bands. The chart gives yellow 4, violet 7, orange multiplier 1000 and gold ±5%. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: 4.7 kΩ; the multiplier can be ignored
options.explanation: Ignoring or changing the multiplier produces the wrong value by an order of magnitude.

options.text: 47 kΩ with ±5% initial tolerance; confirm uncertain colours unpowered out of circuit
options.explanation: Correct. The first two bands form 47, the orange multiplier scales it to kilohms, and gold gives tolerance.

options.text: 473 Ω because the third band is another digit
options.explanation: A four-band part uses two digits, followed by multiplier and tolerance.

options.text: Exactly 47 kΩ in all operating conditions
options.explanation: The marking gives a nominal value and tolerance, not an exact value independent of temperature.

questions.workedExample: Count the bands before interpreting them. This four-band chart uses two significant digits, then a multiplier, then tolerance. That identifies a nominal 47 kΩ resistor with ±5% initial tolerance. Use an unpowered out-of-circuit measurement when colour or orientation is uncertain; the bands do not specify every thermal or power limit.

lessons.title: Preferred resistor values and ratings
lessons.summary: Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result.
lessons.body:
Choosing a resistor means choosing an available value and checking whether the real part can do the job safely. A nominal calculation is the starting point.

## Choose from the table, then check the circuit
Preferred resistor values are published in E-series tables. E12 has twelve values in each tenfold range: 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68 and 82. E24 provides more choices. These series are traditionally associated with 10% and 5% tolerances, but the actual part’s specification determines its tolerance.

The values are approximately evenly spaced in percentage terms. Use the published table rather than generating production values from an approximate geometric formula.

Choose in the direction that suits the circuit. For a resistor limiting nominal LED current, rounding resistance upward reduces current. For a divider or filter, a larger value is not automatically better: check the new ratio or response.

## Nominal value is not an exact value
Component tolerance is the allowed initial departure from the marked resistance. A 10 kΩ ±5% resistor may be 9.5–10.5 kΩ under its specified measurement conditions. Temperature and ageing can add further changes.

For a divider, two resistor errors can reinforce each other: a smaller upper resistor and larger lower resistor raise the output. More precise parts reduce this uncertainty, but do not fix loading or supply variation.

## Check heat and conditions
A resistor dissipation rating specifies the continuous heat allowed under stated thermal conditions. A nominal 0.25 W label does not guarantee that the resistor stays cool, or that the full rating applies at every temperature and mounting arrangement.

Check the circuit using the selected value and tolerance. For an LED resistor, the highest supply, lowest LED forward voltage and lowest allowed resistance give the highest estimated current. Check the corresponding resistor heat, LED limits, GPIO per-pin and total-current limits, and the resistor’s derating curve. A rule such as using half the wattage rating can be a starting margin, but it does not replace those checks.

## Key takeaways

- Select an actual preferred value and reassess the circuit’s behaviour.
- Tolerance and loading are different sources of error.
- Heat, voltage and operating conditions still matter at low supply voltages.

## Further reading

- [Vishay: preferred-value table, IEC 60063](https://www.vishay.com/docs/28372/e-series.pdf)
- [Vishay: resistor colour code](https://www.vishay.com/docs/49411/resistor_color_code_calculator.pdf)
- [OpenStax: electrical energy and power](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-5-electrical-energy-and-power)
- [Vishay MRS16/MRS25: thermal conditions and derating](https://www.vishay.com/docs/28724/mrs16m25.pdf)

questions.prompt: You calculate a resistor value for an LED, then select a nearby preferred value. What should you check next?

options.text: Use the nominal calculation unchanged
options.explanation: The actual chosen value changes current, and tolerances change the worst case.

options.text: Recalculate current and heat using the chosen value and check tolerance and derating
options.explanation: Correct. The preferred value is a real part with limits; confirm both its function and its ratings.

options.text: Ignore the resistor dissipation rating if the supply is below 5 V
options.explanation: Low voltage can still produce enough current to overheat a resistor.

options.text: Choose a smaller resistor to make the LED safest
options.explanation: A smaller series resistance increases current for the same voltage difference.

For a hardware guarantee, check the highest supply voltage, lowest LED forward voltage and lowest resistor value allowed by tolerance. Finally compare resistor heat with the manufacturer’s derating curve at the actual ambient temperature.

lessons.title: Capacitor charging and RC time
lessons.summary: More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current.
lessons.body:
A capacitor stores energy in an electric field by separating charge across an insulating dielectric. Its capacitance, measured in farads, tells you how much charge is needed for a given voltage change.

## Voltage changes need current
An ideal capacitor carries current while its voltage changes. With the same finite charging current, a larger capacitor changes voltage more slowly; with the same capacitor, more current changes it faster. An instantaneous voltage jump would require an idealised infinite current.

At steady DC, an ideal capacitor eventually carries no current while a voltage can remain across it. Real capacitors have leakage and other losses. This makes capacitors useful for coupling changing audio while blocking steady DC, and for supplying brief local current pulses.

For a fixed-current estimate:

```formula reference
ΔV / Δt = I / C
where
ΔV: voltage change across the ideal capacitor, in volts (V)
Δt: duration of that change, in seconds (s)
Δ: change in a quantity
I: constant current entering the positive capacitor terminal, in amperes (A)
C: capacitance, in farads (F)
In words: A larger capacitor changes voltage more slowly for the same charging current. Increasing the current speeds the change; this finite-change expression assumes constant current.
```

## A resistor makes charging slow down
When a DC voltage step charges a capacitor through a resistor, current is largest initially. As the capacitor voltage approaches the supply, less voltage remains across the resistor, so current falls. The curve rises quickly at first and then approaches the final voltage gradually; it is not a straight ramp.

The RC time constant is the characteristic time of that process. Increasing resistance or capacitance makes the response slower. In the ideal initially discharged RC circuit, one time constant takes the voltage about 63.2% of the way to its final value. After five it is about 99.3% there, not exactly finished.

```formula reference
τ = RC
where
τ: tau, the RC time constant, in seconds (s)
R: resistance charging the capacitor, in ohms (Ω)
C: capacitance, in farads (F)
In words: Larger resistance or capacitance stretches the charging and discharging response in time. The product gives the time constant for this ideal RC circuit.
```

A 10 kΩ resistor and 100 nF capacitor have a 1 ms time constant. Doubling either part doubles the time taken to reach the same fraction of the final voltage, without changing that final voltage in this unloaded ideal model. Discharging through a resistor has the same slowing behaviour as the voltage approaches zero.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Filling a wide tank
> At the same inflow, water level rises more slowly in a wide tank than a narrow one.
>
> **How it maps:** Current corresponds to flow rate, capacitor voltage to level, and capacitance to the tank’s capacity per change in level.
>
> **Where it stops:** A capacitor separates electric charge and stores field energy. The tank comparison does not supply a capacitor’s polarity, voltage rating or the exponential RC charging law.

## Key takeaways

- Capacitor voltage changes through current; more capacitance slows a given current’s effect.
- RC charging slows because the resistor’s voltage and current fall as the capacitor charges.
- Time constant describes response speed, not a deadline when charging suddenly stops.

## Further reading

- [OpenStax: ideal RC circuits](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-5-rc-circuits)

questions.prompt: An initially discharged capacitor charges through a resistor from a steady DC supply. Why does its voltage rise quickly at first and then more slowly?

options.text: As capacitor voltage rises, less voltage remains across the resistor, so charging current falls
options.explanation: Correct. The shrinking voltage difference reduces current and therefore the rate of voltage change.

options.text: The resistor gradually runs out of charge
options.explanation: The resistor does not store and consume the charge needed for the process.

options.text: The capacitor always draws the same current until it suddenly stops
options.explanation: Constant current would produce a different charging behaviour; a simple resistor-fed circuit does not hold current constant.

options.text: The supply voltage must be falling
options.explanation: The response occurs even with an ideal supply holding a fixed voltage.

questions.workedExample: Initially the discharged capacitor has little voltage across it, leaving most of the supply across the resistor. Charging raises capacitor voltage and reduces the resistor’s voltage, so current falls. The curve approaches the final supply voltage gradually. A larger resistor or capacitor stretches this process in time.

lessons.title: The RC low-pass cutoff
lessons.summary: More RC smoothing means a slower response.
lessons.body:
An RC low-pass filter smooths changes. A resistor feeds a node with a capacitor to ground, and the output is taken across the capacitor. Slow variations appear largely at the output; rapid variations are reduced because changing the capacitor voltage quickly requires more current.

## Smoothing trades noise for response speed
A knob with unwanted voltage fluctuation can become steadier after RC filtering, but it also takes longer to respond to deliberate movement. Increasing either resistance or capacitance makes the filter slower and lowers its cutoff. Filtering a switch can help with bounce, but the receiver’s threshold and allowed input transition time still matter.

The cutoff is a reference point on a gradual response, not a brick wall. For the ideal unloaded first-order circuit, a sinusoid at cutoff has about 71% of its input amplitude, or −3 dB. Frequencies above it are progressively reduced.

```formula reference
f_c = 1 / (2πRC)
where
f_c: cutoff frequency, in hertz (Hz)
π: pi, approximately 3.14159
R: resistance, in ohms (Ω)
C: capacitance, in farads (F)
In words: Increasing the resistance or capacitance lowers the cutoff, giving more smoothing but a slower response. This formula assumes the ideal output is effectively unloaded.
```

For example, 10 kΩ with 100 nF gives about 159 Hz cutoff. This is a model result, not a measured filter specification. Source resistance, output loading and real component tolerances change the response. A load across the capacitor can change both the low-frequency gain and the cutoff.

## Key takeaways

- More smoothing also slows deliberate changes.
- Cutoff marks gradual attenuation, not an abrupt stop.
- Check loading, input transition and ADC acquisition requirements before relying on the ideal RC model.

## Further reading

- [TI Precision Labs: passive RC response](https://www.ti.com.cn/content/dam/videos/external-videos/zh-cn/4/3816841626001/6119035031001.mp4/subassets/passive_components_and_circuits_2.pdf)
- [OpenStax: ideal RC circuits](https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-5-rc-circuits)
- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)

questions.prompt: A knob’s RC low-pass filter removes jitter but makes deliberate knob movements feel slow. What is the likely effect of reducing capacitance while keeping resistance and loading unchanged?

options.text: Faster response, but less suppression of rapid variations
options.explanation: Correct. Less capacitance raises cutoff and allows faster voltage changes.

options.text: Slower response and more smoothing
options.explanation: That is the effect of increasing capacitance, not reducing it.

options.text: No change because only the resistor sets cutoff
options.explanation: Both resistance and capacitance set the ideal RC response.

options.text: An abrupt cutoff that removes all noise above one frequency
options.explanation: A first-order RC filter has gradual attenuation; changing capacitance does not make it a brick-wall filter.

questions.workedExample: The capacitor must gain or lose charge when the knob changes. With less capacitance, the same current changes its voltage faster, so the filter responds sooner. That also means more rapid unwanted variation passes. Choose the trade-off for the control, and recheck ADC loading and timing requirements.

lessons.title: Capacitor types, component polarity and real capacitance
lessons.summary: Check component polarity and working-voltage limits for the exact part.
lessons.body:
Check component polarity and working-voltage limits for the exact part.

## Types
| Type | Polarised? | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Ceramic (MLCC) | No | Decoupling (often 100 nF), small values |
| Film | No | Audio signal paths, filters |
| Ordinary aluminium electrolytic | **Yes** | Bulk supply filtering, large µF |
| Tantalum | **Yes** | Compact bulk capacitance |

Things to watch:

- **Component polarity.** Ordinary polarised aluminium electrolytic and tantalum capacitors must have their + lead at the higher voltage. Specially specified non-polarised electrolytic types also exist; use each part only as its manufacturer permits. On aluminium electrolytics a stripe marks the **negative** lead, and the negative lead is usually the shorter one. On tantalum capacitors the marking works the other way: a stripe or bar usually marks the **positive** lead. Check the datasheet. Reverse them and they can overheat, vent or burst; tantalums can fail short and catch fire. Don't use a polarised capacitor where the voltage across it can reverse, such as a plain AC audio signal with no DC bias.
- **Voltage rating.** Every capacitor has a maximum working voltage. Choose one comfortably above the highest voltage it will see. For a nominal 5 V rail, establish its highest actual peak before choosing a rating. A 10 V or 16 V part may provide useful margin, but neither a universal multiplier nor the rail’s nominal label establishes suitability. Check ripple current, temperature, lifetime and the manufacturer’s guidance too.
- **Ceramic DC bias.** Many high-value ceramics (X7R, X5R and similar Class 2 dielectrics) lose a significant share of their capacitance when a DC voltage is applied, sometimes well over half near the rated voltage. The effect is documented in manufacturers' DC-bias curves. The "X7R" code itself only describes temperature behaviour (±15% from −55 to +125 °C); it says nothing about voltage. C0G/NP0 (Class 1) ceramics barely change with voltage or temperature, but come in much smaller values than Class 2 types of the same size.
- **Markings.** Small ceramics often use a three-digit code: two digits, then the number of zeros, in picofarads. `104` means 10 followed by four zeros: 100,000 pF, or 100 nF. Treat it as a code to look up, then confirm the part’s voltage rating, dielectric and tolerance from its documentation.

## Key takeaways

- Check component polarity and working-voltage limits for the exact part.
- Use the DC-bias curve for Class 2 ceramic capacitors.

## Further reading

- [Murata: capacitance under an applied DC voltage](https://www.murata.com/en-global/support/faqs/capacitor/ceramiccapacitor/char/0005)
- [Murata: ceramic types and temperature codes](https://go.murata.com/rs/382-MEZ-125/images/AS_2015-008_Continental-2015-2_Email-Thanks_Leaflet_202.pdf)
- [Analog Devices MT-101: decoupling techniques](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-101.pdf)
- [Nichicon: aluminium electrolytic application guidelines](https://www.nichicon.co.jp/english/products/pdf/e-al_gui.pdf)

questions.prompt: An aluminium electrolytic capacitor has a stripe with minus signs down one side. Which lead goes to the more positive voltage?

options.text: The lead under the stripe
options.explanation: The stripe marks the *negative* lead on aluminium electrolytics. Putting it at the higher voltage reverses the capacitor.

options.text: Either: capacitors aren't polarised
options.explanation: Ordinary polarised aluminium electrolytics require the marked polarity. Special non-polar types exist, but that does not make this marked part reversible.

options.text: The lead away from the stripe, usually the longer one
options.explanation: Correct. The stripe marks the negative lead (usually the shorter one), so the other lead is positive.

options.text: The shorter lead
options.explanation: On a new electrolytic the shorter lead is usually the negative one, the same lead the stripe marks.

questions.workedExample:
1. Aluminium electrolytics are polarised: + must sit at the higher voltage.
2. Markings: a stripe (often with − signs) marks the negative lead, which is usually also the shorter lead.
3. So the unmarked, longer lead is positive.
4. Always confirm against the schematic's + symbol before soldering. A reversed electrolytic can vent or burst.

questions.prompt: A bulk electrolytic capacitor will be fitted to a nominal 5 V rail. What must its voltage-rating check account for?

options.text: Only the voltage printed on the supply label
options.explanation: The actual maximum including tolerance, ripple and transients can be higher.

options.text: Only its capacitance in microfarads
options.explanation: Capacitance does not specify the allowed voltage.

options.text: A universal rule that 6.3 V parts are always unsafe on 5 V rails
options.explanation: Suitability depends on actual peak voltage and the exact part’s guidance; a blanket ban is not justified.

options.text: The highest expected voltage including ripple/transients and the manufacturer’s operating guidance
options.explanation: Correct. Choose adequate margin and also check polarity, ripple current, temperature and lifetime requirements.

questions.workedExample: A voltage rating is an operating limit. Establish the highest voltage the capacitor will actually see, including superimposed ripple and transients, then select according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A 10 V or 16 V part may provide useful voltage margin, but rating alone does not establish its suitability.

questions.prompt: You fit a 10 µF X7R ceramic capacitor rated at 6.3 V on a 5 V rail. In circuit, its effective capacitance is far below 10 µF. Why?

options.text: Ceramic capacitors lose capacitance only from age, not from voltage
options.explanation: Ageing is real for Class 2 ceramics, but the dominant effect here is the applied DC voltage.

options.text: It was fitted backwards, so it's acting as a smaller capacitor
options.explanation: Ceramic capacitors aren't polarised. Orientation doesn't change their capacitance.

options.text: Class 2 ceramics such as X7R lose a substantial share of their capacitance under DC bias, especially near their rated voltage
options.explanation: Correct. Check the exact part’s DC-bias curve. A different dielectric, case size or voltage rating may help, but a higher voltage rating alone does not guarantee more retained capacitance.

options.text: The 10 µF marking means 10 µF at 5 V exactly
options.explanation: The nominal value is measured with little or no applied DC-bias voltage. Under that voltage, Class 2 ceramics read lower.

questions.workedExample:
1. X7R, X5R and similar Class 2 ceramics use ferroelectric dielectrics whose permittivity falls as DC field strength rises.
2. At 5 V on a 6.3 V part, the field is high, so the effective capacitance can drop dramatically. Read the manufacturer's DC-bias curve for the exact figure.
3. Compare the actual DC-bias curves of alternatives. A larger case or different part may retain more capacitance; higher voltage rating alone is not a guarantee. C0G/NP0 may not be available in a suitable capacitance or size; an electrolytic has different losses and frequency behaviour.
4. Lesson: the nominal value is a starting point. Check the datasheet curves for real operating conditions.

lessons.title: Choosing an LED’s current-limiting resistor
lessons.summary: Subtract the LED drop before sizing the resistor.
lessons.body:
Subtract the LED drop before sizing the resistor.

## LEDs and the current-limiting resistor
An LED is a diode that emits light. It normally conducts strongly under forward bias and carries much less reverse current within its reverse-voltage limits.
