Its current rises steeply with forward voltage; the quoted **forward voltage** (written V_f) is measured at a stated current rather than being a fixed switching threshold, so an LED always needs something to limit its current, usually a series resistor.

The forward voltage depends on the exact device, current and temperature. For example, Kingbright WP7113ID revision V.14A (8 January 2026) lists 1.9 V typical and 2.3 V maximum at 10 mA (checked 29 October 2026). Those are test conditions, not a recommended drive current or a universal red-LED voltage. Many indicators are useful at only a few milliamps; check the actual LED’s current and thermal limits.

The resistor's job is to take whatever voltage the LED doesn't. Kirchhoff's voltage law gives that leftover voltage, and Ohm's law on the resistor turns it into a resistance:

```formula reference
R = (V_supply − V_f) / I_LED
where
R: nominal series resistance, in ohms (Ω)
V_supply: supply or loaded pin voltage, in volts (V)
V_f: assumed LED forward voltage at the chosen current, in volts
I_LED: desired LED current, in amperes (A)
In words: The resistor takes the voltage left after the LED’s forward drop. A larger resistance gives less current for the same assumed voltage difference; the LED’s drop is not a fixed threshold.
```

With assumed 3.3 V drive and 2.0 V LED drop, a nominal 5 mA target calls for 260 Ω. The next E12 value up, 270 Ω, gives about 4.81 mA and 6.26 mW resistor heat under those same assumptions. Choosing a larger preferred value reduces nominal current; it does not by itself prove a worst-case safe design.

For a hardware bound, use maximum supply, minimum LED drop and minimum resistance allowed by tolerance. Check resistor heat, LED thermal/current limits and the source’s loaded output voltage. A GPIO also has per-pin and combined pin-current limits; a nominal estimate below one limit is not enough if variation can exceed it.

**LED orientation:** the longer leg is usually the anode (+). The cathode (−) is often marked by a flat on the rim. Check the datasheet. Reversed, it may stay dark but may also exceed its allowed reverse voltage. Do not apply a reverse voltage beyond the exact LED’s rating. LED reverse ratings are often only a few volts.

## Key takeaways

- Subtract the LED drop before sizing the resistor.
- Use worst-case supply, forward voltage and resistor tolerance for hardware.

## Further reading

- [Kingbright WP7113ID, revision V.14A](https://www.kingbrightusa.com/images/catalog/spec/wp7113id.pdf)
- [Kingbright WP7113QBC/D, revision V.18B](https://www.kingbrightusa.com/images/catalog/spec/wp7113qbc-d.pdf)
- [SparkFun: LED current limiting](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/light-emitting-diodes-leds/all)

questions.prompt: Your nominal LED calculation calls for a resistor between two available preferred values. You want nominal current no greater than the target. Which is the better next step?

options.text: Choose the lower value because less resistance protects the LED
options.explanation: Less resistance normally increases current for the same source and assumed LED drop.

options.text: Ignore the LED drop and always use the full supply voltage
options.explanation: The resistor takes only the remaining supply voltage in the series model.

options.text: Choose the next higher resistance, then recheck actual current, heat and worst-case limits
options.explanation: Correct. Upward rounding reduces nominal current, but tolerances and voltage variation still need checks.

options.text: Choose either neighbour because resistor value does not affect current
options.explanation: Changing the resistor changes the current-setting path.

questions.workedExample: Use the voltage left after the assumed LED forward drop when selecting the nominal resistance. A higher resistance reduces current under those assumptions. Then check maximum source voltage, minimum LED drop, minimum resistor tolerance, LED/GPIO current limits and resistor dissipation. A nominal target is not a worst-case guarantee.

questions.prompt: An LED itself permits more current than the GPIO pin that drives it. A nominal design already exceeds the pin’s documented limit. What should change?

options.text: Nothing, because only the LED’s rating matters
options.explanation: Both the source pin and LED must operate within their own limits.

options.text: Reduce the drive current or use an appropriate external driver, then check all relevant limits
options.explanation: Correct. The GPIO can be the limiting component even if the LED could carry more current.

options.text: Use a smaller series resistor to protect the pin
options.explanation: A smaller resistance increases current and worsens the overload.

options.text: Keep the circuit because a nominally correct LED voltage guarantees pin safety
options.explanation: Forward voltage is not a current regulator or a guarantee of safe GPIO loading.

questions.workedExample: The current path includes the GPIO, resistor and LED, so every part must be suitable. Reduce current with a properly selected resistor, or use a documented driver if more LED current is needed. Check loaded output voltage, per-pin and combined pin current, tolerances, LED limits and resistor heat; do not treat absolute maximum ratings as targets.

lessons.title: Diode direction, drops and protection
lessons.summary: A diode’s current and temperature affect its forward drop.
lessons.body:
A diode’s current and temperature affect its forward drop.

## Diodes
A forward-biased diode conducts conventional current from **anode** to **cathode** (towards the bar in its schematic symbol; an LED’s outward arrows represent emitted light). Reverse-biased, it normally carries a small leakage current until breakdown; respect the exact reverse-voltage rating. The cathode is marked with a band.

| Type | Forward drop (approx.) | Common use |
|---|---|---|
| Silicon (e.g. 1N4148) | ~0.6–0.75 V at a few mA | Low-current signal switching, diode clamping |
| Silicon rectifier (e.g. 1N400x) | ~0.7 V small current, up to ~1 V at 1 A | Reverse-polarity protection |
| Schottky | ~0.2–0.4 V small current, ~0.45–0.6 V at 1 A | Low-drop protection |

The forward drops are approximate, and they rise with current and fall with temperature. Datasheets give limits at stated test conditions and show typical curves. Checked 29 October 2026: Vishay 1N4148 revision 1.6 (7 November 2024) gives 1 V maximum at 10 mA; Vishay 1N5817 revision 1 July 2020 gives 0.45 V maximum at 1 A, while Vishay 1N4001–1N4007 revision 29 April 2020 gives 1.1 V maximum at 1 A. These are exact documented examples, not a universal diode drop.

Uses in a synth:

- **Reverse-polarity protection:** a series diode in the supply line blocks current if the supply is connected backwards, at the cost of its forward drop.
- **Diode clamping:** diodes to the supply rails catch input overvoltage (the logic and datasheet units).
- **Flyback:** a correctly oriented diode across a DC relay or motor coil lets its current recirculate after switch-off, limiting the voltage spike while stored magnetic energy is dissipated. Check the drive circuit and release-time requirements.

When checking orientation, use the exact part’s markings: an LED’s longer lead is usually its anode, and an axial diode’s band marks the cathode. Ordinary ceramic capacitors are non-polarised; tantalum capacitors are polarised and must not be reversed. Lead length alone is unreliable after leads have been trimmed.

## Key takeaways

- A diode’s current and temperature affect its forward drop.
- Check component polarity and reverse ratings; a diode does not eliminate all fault paths.

## Further reading

- [Vishay 1N4148, revision 1.6](https://www.vishay.com/docs/81857/1n4148.pdf)
- [Vishay 1N4001–1N4007, revision 29 April 2020](https://www.vishay.com/docs/88503/1n4001.pdf)
- [Vishay 1N5817–1N5819, revision 1 July 2020](https://www.vishay.com/docs/88525/1n5817.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which statements about component polarity are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An LED's longer leg is usually the anode (+)
options.explanation: Correct. It's the usual convention, though a datasheet or a quick test with a meter's diode mode confirms it.

options.text: The band on a diode marks the cathode
options.explanation: Correct. Conventional current flows from anode to the banded cathode when the diode is forward biased.

options.text: Ceramic 100 nF decoupling capacitors must be fitted with the right component polarity
options.explanation: Ceramic capacitors aren't polarised; either orientation works.

options.text: A tantalum capacitor can be fitted either way round
options.explanation: Tantalum capacitors are polarised, like aluminium electrolytics. Reverse voltage can cause failure.

questions.workedExample:
Go through the parts:

- LED: polarised; long leg usually the anode, flat rim on the cathode side. True.
- Diode: band = cathode. True.
- Ceramic (MLCC): not polarised. False.
- Tantalum: polarised. False.

Rule: before power-up, check every polarised part against the schematic.

lessons.title: Switch contacts and connector pinouts
lessons.summary: Poles and throws describe routing; momentary describes spring return.
lessons.body:
Poles and throws describe routing; momentary describes spring return.

## Switches and buttons
Switches are described by their poles and throws: **switch poles** are the independent circuits switched, and **switch throws** are the positions each pole can connect to.

- **SPST:** single pole, single throw. A simple on/off.
- **SPDT:** single pole, double throw. A common terminal switches between two others.
- **DPDT:** two SPDT switches moved together.

**Momentary switches** spring back when released; a normally open push button connects while pressed, whereas a normally closed one opens. **Latching switches** stay in the selected state. Toggle describes the actuator, and toggle switches can be latching or momentary. Tactile buttons often have four legs that are internally connected in pairs. Check which pairs with a continuity tester before wiring.

Mechanical contacts **bounce** (contact bounce): for a few milliseconds a press looks like several rapid presses. A microcontroller reading a button also needs a defined idle level from a pull-up or pull-down resistor. Debouncing and pull-ups are covered with the embedded topics.

## Connectors and pinouts
Connectors are where parts are most often wired wrong.

- **Pin headers** are commonly on a 2.54 mm (0.1 in) contact spacing. Pin 1 is marked by a square pad, a triangle or a dot.
- **Pinout diagrams can be drawn from either side.** "Looking into the socket" and "looking at the solder side" are mirror images. Check which view the diagram shows.
- **Audio jacks:** on a 3.5 mm or 6.35 mm TRS stereo jack, the tip carries left, the ring carries right and the sleeve is ground. On a mono TS jack, the tip carries the signal and the sleeve is ground.
- **Connector keying:** keyed connectors only fit one way. Unkeyed headers fit both ways, including the wrong one.
- **Product-specific connectors** (power inputs, MIDI DIN, board edge headers) have pinouts defined by the product or standard. Take them from that documentation, never from memory. DIN MIDI isn't a direct GPIO connection; it needs the interface circuit from the MIDI specification, covered in a later module.

> [!warning] Component polarity and pinout mistakes destroy parts
> Before power-up, check every polarised part (electrolytics, diodes, LEDs, chips) and every connector orientation against the schematic. It takes a minute and catches the most common fatal mistakes.

## Key takeaways

- Poles and throws describe routing; momentary describes spring return.
- Confirm both internal switch contacts and the view used for a connector pinout.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: reading schematics](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-read-a-schematic/all)
- [SparkFun: breadboard connections](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-breadboard/all)
- [RaneNote 110: system interconnection](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note110.html)

questions.prompt: A front-panel switch needs to route a signal to either output A or output B. Which switch type does that with one moving contact?

options.text: SPST
options.explanation: Single throw means only on/off on one path. It can't choose between two destinations.

options.text: SPDT
options.explanation: Correct. Single pole, double throw: one common terminal connects to one of two others.

options.text: DPST
options.explanation: Double pole, single throw switches two separate circuits on and off together. It still has no second position to route to.

options.text: An SPST momentary push button
options.explanation: Momentary refers to spring return, not routing. A typical momentary button is SPST.

questions.workedExample:
1. Poles = independent circuits switched; throws = positions each pole can connect to.
2. You need one circuit (one pole) choosing between two destinations (two throws).
3. That's SPDT: the common terminal connects to A in one position and B in the other.
4. For stereo (two signals switched together) you'd use DPDT.

questions.prompt: Which statements about connectors and pinouts are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: On a TRS stereo jack, the tip carries left, the ring right, and the sleeve is ground
options.explanation: Correct. That's the standard stereo convention.

options.text: A pinout drawn "looking into the socket" is a mirror image of one drawn from the solder side
options.explanation: Correct. Always check which view a diagram uses before soldering.

options.text: An unkeyed 2.54 mm header can only be plugged in the correct way
options.explanation: Unkeyed headers fit either way round, including the wrong one. Mark pin 1 on both halves.

options.text: DIN MIDI can be wired straight to any microcontroller GPIO pin
options.explanation: DIN MIDI needs the interface circuit from the MIDI specification. It isn't a direct GPIO connection.

questions.workedExample:
1. TRS: tip, ring and sleeve carry left, right and ground for stereo audio. True.
2. Views: a connector seen from the front and from the back are mirror images, so pin numbering appears reversed. True.
3. Unkeyed headers can be reversed. False.
4. DIN MIDI needs a documented interface circuit. False.

questions.prompt: You wire a normally open four-legged tactile button between a GPIO input with an enabled pull-up and ground. The input reads "pressed" all the time, even with nothing touched. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The button is faulty out of the box
options.explanation: Possible but unlikely. The usual cause is wiring, and you should check that first.

options.text: The button bounces
options.explanation: Bounce lasts milliseconds after a press. It doesn't make the input read pressed permanently.

options.text: Buttons need a capacitor to work
options.explanation: A capacitor can help with debouncing, but its absence doesn't make the button read pressed all the time.

options.text: You used two legs that are internally connected, so the pin is permanently shorted to ground
options.explanation: Correct. Tactile buttons usually have two pairs of legs joined internally. Wiring across a joined pair makes a permanent connection. Use legs from different pairs, and confirm with a continuity test.

questions.workedExample:
1. A four-leg tactile switch has two contacts, each reached through a pair of legs joined inside the package.
2. If both wires go to the same internal pair, the pin connects to ground whatever the button does.
3. Diagnose with power off: continuity between the two legs you used, button released. Check the resistance and switch state; a low reading consistent with a direct connection supports the diagnosis.
4. Fix: move one wire to a leg from the other pair, as confirmed by the exact switch pinout. Then confirm continuity only when pressed.

lessons.title: Supply pins, signal limits and stress ratings
lessons.summary: A board’s power input does not specify its I/O voltage tolerance.
lessons.body:
The fastest way to destroy a microcontroller board is to connect something at the wrong voltage. This lesson covers how to know, from the documents, what each pin will accept, and how to make two parts with different supplies talk safely.

> [!warning] Scope
> Everything here concerns low-voltage DC logic and audio circuits, typically 3.3 V and 5 V. Power your circuits from a certified USB supply or bench supply. Mains power-supply design is out of scope.

## Supply voltages: 3.3 V and 5 V
Two supply voltages dominate hobby digital electronics:

- **5 V:** a common board-input supply, including ordinary USB-powered examples in this module, and the native supply of older logic families and many classic microcontrollers.
- **3.3 V:** a common supply for modern microcontrollers, including the ARM chips on audio-focused boards.

Many boards accept 5 V from USB and use an on-board **voltage regulator** to make 3.3 V for the chip. The board may expose both voltages on pins. **The fact that 5 V exists on the board says nothing about whether the chip's I/O pins tolerate 5 V.**

> [!example] A real board's limits
> PJRC’s Teensy 4.1 product documentation (checked 29 October 2026; this page does not identify a separate PCB revision) states that its digital pins accept 0 to 3.3 V signals and "are not 5V tolerant", and that the analogue range is fixed at 0 to 3.3 V. Other boards differ: some microcontrollers have individual 5 V-tolerant pins. Read the exact board and revision's documentation and the microcontroller datasheet, and record the date you checked.

## Absolute maximum ratings versus recommended operating conditions
Every datasheet separates two very different tables.

**Absolute Maximum Ratings** describe stress limits, not guaranteed operation. Exceeding them can cause permanent damage; extended operation at those limits can reduce reliability. TI’s SN74HC00 datasheet SCLS181H (revision H, August 2021; checked 29 October 2026) includes a supply maximum of 7 V and an input clamp current of ±20 mA.

**Recommended Operating Conditions** are where the part is guaranteed to work as specified: for the SN74HC00, a supply (V_CC) from 2 V to 6 V, with inputs between 0 V and the supply voltage.

```diagram
 0V                                    7V
 |--- recommended: 2–6 V ---|          |
 |------- stress limit: 7 V -----------|
    not a guaranteed operating range
```

Design inside recommended conditions with margin. Never treat an absolute maximum as a target. Living near it can shorten the part's life even if it doesn't fail at once.

## Key takeaways

- A board’s power input does not specify its I/O voltage tolerance.
- Design inside recommended conditions, not at absolute maximum ratings.

## Further reading

- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)
- [PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)

questions.prompt: A datasheet lists a supply voltage of 2–6 V under Recommended Operating Conditions and 7 V under Absolute Maximum Ratings. What supply should you design for?

options.text: 7 V, the highest the part supports
options.explanation: 7 V is a stress limit beyond which damage may occur. Operation there isn't guaranteed, and parts living near it may have shorter lives.

options.text: Anywhere up to 7 V, since both tables say it's fine
options.explanation: Only the recommended table guarantees function. Between 6 V and 7 V the part may survive but isn't specified to work.

options.text: Within 2–6 V, with some margin from the edges
options.explanation: Correct. Recommended Operating Conditions define where the part is guaranteed to meet its specifications. Absolute maximums are damage thresholds, not operating points.

options.text: Exactly 2 V, to minimise stress
options.explanation: 2 V is the edge of the range, with no margin for supply droop. Pick a supply comfortably inside the range, such as 5 V here.

questions.workedExample:
1. Absolute Maximum Ratings: TI's wording is that exceeding them "may cause permanent damage", and that they are "stress ratings only" which don't imply functional operation.
2. Recommended Operating Conditions: the range where electrical characteristics are guaranteed.
3. Design inside the recommended range with margin for tolerance and droop. For the SN74HC00, 5 V sits nicely inside 2–6 V.

questions.prompt: A Teensy 4.1 is powered from USB (5 V). You want to connect a 5 V logic output to one of its digital pins. According to PJRC's documentation (checked October 2026), is that safe?

options.text: Yes, because the board runs from 5 V USB
options.explanation: The board *accepts* 5 V power and regulates it down. Its I/O pins are 3.3 V only.

options.text: Yes, if the pin is configured as an input
options.explanation: Configuration doesn't change the electrical rating. PJRC says the pins aren't 5 V tolerant regardless.

options.text: Only for analogue pins
options.explanation: PJRC says the analogue pins aren't 5 V tolerant either. Their range is fixed at 0 to 3.3 V.

options.text: No. PJRC states the pins accept 0 to 3.3 V and are not 5 V tolerant, so level-shift the signal down first
options.explanation: Correct. Use a level shifter or a suitable divider, and recheck the current documentation for your exact board revision.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the board's *power input* from its *I/O ratings*.
2. PJRC specifies a 0–3.3 V signal range for Teensy 4.1 and expressly excludes 5 V tolerance. That signal limit applies even when USB supplies the board’s power.
3. So a 5 V output needs level shifting before it reaches the pin.
4. Product details change between models and revisions. Check the current page for your exact board.

lessons.title: Logic thresholds and noise margins
lessons.summary: Compare worst-case output levels with guaranteed input thresholds.
lessons.body:
Compare worst-case output levels with guaranteed input thresholds.

## Logic levels and thresholds
A digital input interprets voltage as high or low. Its datasheet gives guaranteed input regions; the actual switching point may vary between devices and conditions. All inputs must also stay within their permitted voltage range.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| V_IH(min) | Lowest voltage guaranteed read as high |
| V_IL(max) | Highest voltage guaranteed read as low |
| V_OH(min) | Lowest voltage a high output guarantees |
| V_OL(max) | Highest voltage a low output guarantees |

Between V_IL(max) and V_IH(min) is a forbidden zone where the input's behaviour isn't guaranteed.

An output can drive an input reliably only if the worst-case output always lands inside the region the input is guaranteed to accept, in both states.

The weakest guaranteed high from the driver must reach at least the receiver’s high threshold. The highest guaranteed low from the driver must stay at or below the receiver’s low threshold. Check both states under the actual supply, load and temperature conditions.

The gaps between the two sides are the **noise margins**: how much noise (or ground offset) the link can tolerate before a bit is misread:

```formula reference
NM_H = V_{OH(min)} − V_{IH(min)}
NM_L = V_{IL(max)} − V_{OL(max)}
where
NM_H: high-state static noise margin, in volts (V)
NM_L: low-state static noise margin, in volts
V_{OH(min)}: minimum guaranteed driver high voltage, in volts
V_{IH(min)}: receiver’s minimum guaranteed high-input voltage, in volts
V_{IL(max)}: receiver’s maximum guaranteed low-input voltage, in volts
V_{OL(max)}: maximum guaranteed driver low voltage, in volts
In words: Each margin is the distance inside a guaranteed input region. Positive margin allows some noise and ground offset; negative margin gives no guarantee. Timing and voltage stress must still be checked.
```

A driver guaranteed high at 2.4 V or above has room above a receiver’s 2.0 V high threshold. A 0.4 V maximum low also fits below a 0.8 V low threshold. Each leaves 0.4 V static margin; a disturbance larger than that can leave the guaranteed region without necessarily causing a particular chip to switch.

## Key takeaways

- Compare driver and receiver guarantees for both states.
- A positive static margin is a budget for specified noise and ground offset; electrical stress and timing still need separate checks.

## Further reading

- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)
- [TI SN74HCT00, manufacturer datasheet](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hct00.pdf)
- [TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/szza036c/szza036c.pdf)

questions.prompt: A driver guarantees high at least 2.4 V and low at most 0.4 V. The receiver guarantees high from 2.0 V and low up to 0.8 V, within its permitted input range. What can you conclude?

options.text: The complete interface is guaranteed at every speed
options.explanation: Static voltage compatibility does not establish edge-rate, timing or loading compatibility.

options.text: Both static states have positive margin under these conditions; stress and timing still need checks
options.explanation: Correct. Each worst-case output lies inside the corresponding guaranteed input region.

options.text: The high must be compared with the receiver’s low threshold
options.explanation: High outputs must meet the high threshold, and low outputs the low threshold.

options.text: A signal above 2.0 V is safe even if it exceeds the receiver’s voltage rating
options.explanation: A logic threshold is not an overvoltage rating.

questions.workedExample: Compare like states. The weakest guaranteed high is above the high threshold, and the highest guaranteed low is below the low threshold. That leaves some room for noise and reference offset. These guarantees only apply under their stated load, supply and temperature conditions, and do not replace timing or stress checks.

lessons.title: Interfacing HC and HCT logic
lessons.summary: Compare actual HC and HCT thresholds before translating logic levels.
lessons.body:
Use the threshold and noise-margin definitions from the preceding unit to choose an interface. The output limits in this example are illustrative driver guarantees: a high of at least 2.4 V and a low of at most 0.4 V. Check the real part’s load, supply, temperature, edge rates and receiving voltage limits.

## HC and HCT threshold examples

| Part (supply) | Reads high from | Reads low up to |
|---|---|---|
| SN74HC00 (4.5 V) | 3.15 V | 1.35 V |
| SN74HCT00 (4.5–5.5 V) | 2.0 V | 0.8 V |

Checked 29 October 2026: these examples use TI SN74HC00 datasheet SCLS181H (revision H, August 2021) and SN74HCT00 datasheet SCLS062F (revision F, October 2022). The SN74HC00 figures come from its datasheet (Recommended Operating Conditions with a 4.5 V supply). HC input thresholds scale with the supply voltage. The SN74HCT00 figures are "TTL-compatible" thresholds, designed to accept lower-voltage highs.

Suppose a 3.3 V microcontroller output guarantees a high of at least 2.4 V and a low of at most 0.4 V. These are illustrative output guarantees for this calculation, not a specification for an arbitrary microcontroller. Take the real ones from your chip's datasheet at your load current, then compare them with each receiver.

The illustrative 2.4 V guaranteed high falls below the HC input’s 3.15 V requirement, so that state is not guaranteed. The 0.4 V low satisfies its 1.35 V low limit. HCT accepts both: its 2.0 V high threshold and 0.8 V low limit each leave 0.4 V static margin for this driver.

The negative high margin means a 3.3 V output **isn't guaranteed** to be read as high by a 5 V HC input. It may work on your bench and fail on another day or another chip. The HCT part has positive margins in both states, which is why an HCT buffer powered from 5 V is a standard way to translate 3.3 V logic up to 5 V. TI's HCT application note (SCLA011) recommends HCT parts for the closely related problem of feeding TTL-level outputs into HC logic.

### The dangerous direction: 5 V into 3.3 V

Going down is the real hazard. A 5 V output driving a 3.3 V-only input exceeds that input's rating. Options, depending on speed and direction:

- A **level-shifter** chip designed for the job (the robust choice for fast or bidirectional signals).
- A **voltage divider** (two resistors) to scale 5 V down to about 3.3 V, for slow, one-way signals. The divider-loading rules from the earlier divider lessons apply.
- An input the datasheet explicitly specifies as 5 V tolerant, under the stated conditions.

## Key takeaways

- HCT inputs can accept the example driver’s lower high voltage when every stated condition is satisfied.
- Going from a 5 V output to a 3.3 V-only input needs documented level conversion; the board supply does not establish I/O tolerance.

## Further reading

- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)
- [TI SN74HCT00, manufacturer datasheet](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hct00.pdf)
- [TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/szza036c/szza036c.pdf)

questions.prompt: A 3.3 V microcontroller (guaranteed high of at least 2.4 V and low of at most 0.4 V under the stated load) must drive a 74HC chip powered at 4.5 V. With a 4.5 V supply, TI's SN74HC00 only guarantees to read 3.15 V or more as high. What's the best approach?

options.text: Connect directly; it worked on the bench
options.explanation: A bench test proves one chip on one day. The worst-case high (2.4 V) is below 3.15 V, so it isn't guaranteed.

options.text: Add a series resistor
options.explanation: A series resistor limits current. It can't raise a voltage to meet the input's high threshold.

options.text: Use a suitable HCT input stage on the receiver’s 4.5 V supply, or a specified level shifter
options.explanation: Correct. SN74HCT00 accepts a high from 2.0 V at a 4.5–5.5 V supply, giving 0.4 V of high margin for this driver. Check both states, output loading, edge rates, supply tolerance and receiving voltage limits; a separate 5 V output must not overdrive a 4.5 V-only receiver.

options.text: Power the 74HC from 3.3 V but keep its outputs driving the same 4.5 V HC inputs
options.explanation: Powered from 3.3 V, the 74HC's outputs only reach about 3.3 V, which moves the compatibility problem to the next stage.

questions.workedExample: The illustrative driver’s 2.4 V minimum high is below the HC receiver’s 3.15 V guaranteed high threshold, even though its low state fits. A bench success cannot extend the guarantee. A suitable HCT stage has lower input-high requirements, but its supply, both output states, load and timing must match the next stage too. Here a valid shared 4.5 V supply avoids adding a separate 5 V output that might overdrive a 4.5 V-only receiver. A specified level shifter is another option.

lessons.title: Reading a datasheet’s guarantees
lessons.summary: Match part, package, view, temperature, supply and load conditions.
lessons.body:
Match part, package, view, temperature, supply and load conditions.

## Reading a datasheet
Datasheets follow a predictable layout. In order of usefulness to a beginner:

1. **Features and description:** what the part is, supply range, key specs.
2. **Pin configuration:** pin numbers and names. Note which **view** (top view is standard for ICs) and the pin 1 marking.
3. **Absolute maximum ratings:** stress limits, not guaranteed operating conditions.
4. **Recommended operating conditions:** where to design.
5. **Electrical characteristics:** guaranteed min/max values under stated **test conditions**, such as V_OH at a given load current.
6. **Typical characteristics (graphs):** how the part usually behaves. Not guaranteed.
7. **Application and layout information:** example circuits, decoupling and layout advice. Often the most practical section.

Rules of thumb:

- **Design to min/max, not "typ".** Typical values describe representative behaviour under the stated conditions and are not production guarantees.
- **Read the test conditions.** A guaranteed minimum high output at 20 µA isn't the same as at 4 mA. TI's SN74HC00 lists 4.4 V and 3.98 V respectively, with a 4.5 V supply at 25 °C.
- **Read the footnotes.** They hold the exceptions.
- **Get the datasheet for the exact part number**, including suffixes, from the manufacturer.

## Key takeaways

- Match part, package, view, temperature, supply and load conditions.
- Typical curves describe behaviour but are not guaranteed limits.

## Further reading

- [TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/szza036c/szza036c.pdf)
- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)

questions.prompt: A datasheet's electrical characteristics list an output's high voltage as min 3.98 V, typ 4.3 V at 4 mA load. Which value should your design rely on?

options.text: 4.3 V, because it's what most parts do
options.explanation: Typical values aren't guaranteed. Some parts will be lower, and a design relying on typ fails on those.

options.text: 3.98 V, the guaranteed minimum under those test conditions
options.explanation: Correct. Design to guaranteed limits under conditions matching your circuit, here a 4 mA load at that supply and temperature.

options.text: The supply voltage, since CMOS outputs swing rail to rail
options.explanation: Under load, an output voltage falls below the rail. The table quantifies how far.

options.text: The average of min and typ
options.explanation: Averaging guaranteed and typical values gives a figure with no guarantee at all.

questions.workedExample:
1. Min/max values are guaranteed (tested or guaranteed by design) under the stated conditions.
2. Typ describes a typical part and isn't guaranteed.
3. Match the test conditions: this is the high output voltage at 4 mA, so it applies if your load draws about 4 mA or less.
4. For TI's SN74HC00 with a 4.5 V supply at 25 °C, the guaranteed minimum high output is 4.4 V at 20 µA but 3.98 V at 4 mA. The load matters.

questions.prompt: When reading a pin diagram in an IC datasheet, what must you check before wiring?

options.text: Nothing: pin 1 is always top left of the drawing
options.explanation: Drawings can be top or bottom views. If you assume the wrong one, the pins come out mirrored.

options.text: Which view it shows (usually top view) and how pin 1 is marked on the physical part
options.explanation: Correct. Datasheets label the view. Match the physical pin 1 marker (dot, notch or bevel) to the drawing.

options.text: Only the supply pins, because signal pins are interchangeable
options.explanation: Signal pins have distinct functions, and swapping them breaks the circuit.

options.text: The typical characteristics graphs
options.explanation: Useful for behaviour, but irrelevant to which physical pin is which.

questions.workedExample:
1. Find the view label: "top view" is standard for IC packages.
2. Find pin 1 on the part: a dot, notch or bevel.
3. Count pins anticlockwise from pin 1 when looking at the top of a DIP or SOIC package.
4. Wrong-view mistakes mirror the pinout, often putting power on a signal pin.

lessons.title: Level conversion, input clamps and back-powering
lessons.summary: Use proper level conversion during normal operation.
lessons.body:
Use proper level conversion during normal operation.

## Protecting inputs
Inputs that connect to the outside world (jacks, long wires, other equipment) see accidents: wrong voltages, static discharge, hot-plugging.

Many CMOS inputs, including the SN74HC00, have internal **clamp diodes** from each input to the supply pin (V_CC) and to GND. When an input goes beyond a rail by a diode drop, the diode conducts and dumps the excess current into the rail.

```diagram
        VCC
         |
        ─┴─ clamp diode
  in ─[ R ]─┬──── chip input
        ─┬─ clamp diode
         |
        GND
```

A **series resistor** limits the current that flows into those clamps during a fault. TI permits particular over-rail cases only when its specified pin-current limits are observed; that exception belongs to this exact device, not every microcontroller. During a fault the clamp holds the pin about one diode drop above the rail, so the resistor takes the rest of the fault voltage.

A larger series resistance reduces fault current for the same voltage difference. But current diverted into a supply rail must go somewhere: a lightly loaded regulator may not absorb it, allowing the rail to rise. An unpowered chip can also be partly powered through this path.

A real protection design needs the diode’s voltage-current behaviour, resistor tolerance, rail behaviour and the exact chip’s voltage and injection-current limits. A small calculated current alone does not establish safety.

Be conservative:

- **Clamps are fault protection, not a level shifter.** Some manufacturers, such as PJRC for Teensy 4.1, say plainly not to drive pins above 3.3 V. Use proper level conversion for normal operation.
- **Microcontrollers specify their own injected-current limits.** Check the chip's datasheet rather than borrowing a 74HC figure.
- **Back-powering:** a signal driven into an unpowered chip can power it partly through the clamp diodes, causing strange behaviour or damage. Power boards up together, or make sure signals can't arrive before the supply.
- **External Schottky clamps** may divert current before internal diodes, but only if their actual drop at the relevant current is low enough. Check leakage, capacitance, fault ratings and where the rail current goes.

## Key takeaways

- Use proper level conversion during normal operation.
- Clamp current and supply-rail injection must both remain within documented limits.

## Further reading

- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)
- [TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/szza036c/szza036c.pdf)
- [PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits](https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy41.html)

questions.prompt: Which are acceptable ways to feed a 5 V logic signal into a 3.3 V-only input in normal operation? Select all that apply.

options.text: A level-shifter chip designed for 5 V to 3.3 V translation
options.explanation: Correct. It's the robust choice, especially for fast or bidirectional signals.

options.text: A resistor divider scaling 5 V to about 3.3 V, for a slow one-way signal
options.explanation: Correct, with the caveats from the divider units: it loads the source, and its resistance with the input capacitance slows edges.

options.text: A direct wire, because the input's clamp diodes will handle it
options.explanation: Clamp diodes are fault protection, not a design feature. Some vendors, including PJRC for Teensy 4.1, say never to drive pins above 3.3 V.

options.text: A 10 kΩ series resistor alone, relying on the clamp diodes in normal operation
options.explanation: That limits fault current but still pushes current into the clamps continuously. Treat it as protection, not level conversion.

questions.workedExample: Normal operation must keep the input within its documented range. A suitable level shifter can provide that conversion. A divider can work for a slow one-way signal only after checking worst-case high and low levels, resistor tolerances, loading, input capacitance, edge-rate requirements and powered-off behaviour. A series resistor alone does not lower an unloaded input voltage; relying on input clamps can inject current into a rail and may violate the exact device’s limits.

questions.prompt: A resistor limits current into an input clamp during an overvoltage fault. The calculated current is below the assumed diode limit. Why is that not enough to declare the circuit protected?

options.text: A resistor has no effect on clamp current
options.explanation: A resistor does limit current, but that is only one requirement.

options.text: A clamp always absorbs all fault energy without affecting other circuitry
options.explanation: Clamp current must go somewhere, often into a supply rail that may be unable to sink it.

options.text: Diode forward voltage is fixed and independent of current
options.explanation: Forward drop varies with current, temperature and device, so assumed values need checking.

options.text: Pin voltage, injection limits, component tolerances and supply-rail behaviour must also be safe
options.explanation: Correct. A small calculated current can still violate a pin-voltage rule, raise the rail or back-power an unpowered chip.

questions.workedExample: Trace the fault current beyond the diode. It may enter a rail whose regulator cannot absorb it, raising the rail or partly powering a chip. Check the exact pin-voltage and injected-current limits, diode behaviour, resistor tolerance and powered-off conditions. Use proper normal-operation level conversion; the illustrative clamp-current model is not a universal protection recipe.

questions.prompt: Your synth board is switched off but connected by a data cable to a powered board. Its power LED continues to glow faintly while that cable is attached and goes out when you unplug it. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Back-powering: signals from the powered board flow through input clamp diodes into the unpowered board's supply rail
options.explanation: Correct. The clamp from the input to the supply pin conducts when the input is above the unpowered rail, partly powering the chip and its rail. This can cause erratic behaviour or damage.

options.text: The off switch is broken
options.explanation: Possible, but the classic cause of a faint glow from a connected, unpowered board is back-powering through signal pins.

options.text: Capacitors still hold charge from earlier
options.explanation: Stored charge can keep an LED glowing briefly after switch-off, but it decays. A glow sustained by the attached powered cable points to an external current path.

options.text: Ground loops always light LEDs
options.explanation: A ground loop does not automatically light a power LED. Here the sustained glow depends on the powered data cable, consistent with current entering a supply rail through a signal-pin path.

questions.workedExample:
1. Many CMOS inputs have a clamp diode to the chip's supply pin (V_CC).
2. Unpowered, that supply rail sits at about 0 V. A high signal from the other board forward-biases the diode.
3. Current flows into the unpowered rail, which rises enough to light an LED and partly run chips.
4. Fixes: power both boards together; series resistors can reduce current but do not by themselves guarantee safe powered-off behaviour; use buffers or level shifters specified for powered-off inputs; or sequence power. Check the chip datasheet for powered-off input behaviour.

lessons.title: Local decoupling and bulk supply storage
lessons.summary: A local capacitor shortens the path for switching current pulses.
lessons.body:
A local capacitor shortens the path for switching current pulses.

## Decoupling capacitors
Digital chips draw current in very short pulses each time their transistors switch. The supply wiring has resistance and inductance, so it can't deliver those pulses instantly. The local supply voltage dips and rings, and that noise spreads to everything sharing the supply, including audio.

A **decoupling capacitor** (bypass capacitor) next to the chip's supply pin acts as a local reservoir, supplying the pulses so the long supply path doesn't have to. For TI SN74HC00, datasheet SCLS181H recommends 0.1 µF at the supply terminal, allows combining it with 1 µF to address different noise frequencies, and places bypass capacitors close to the supply terminal.

Practical rules:

- **Use each device’s specified local capacitors.** For SN74HC00, the documented 100 nF capacitor goes close to its supply pin, with short connections to the pin and to ground. Distance adds inductance and defeats the purpose.
- **Bulk capacitance** (an electrolytic, say 10–100 µF) where power enters a board, for slower load changes. Values are typical, not prescriptive; follow the datasheets.
- **Follow the datasheet** where it gives specific values. Audio codecs and regulators often do.

The noise and grounding units explain why this matters even more for audio.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A nearby water bottle
> A nearby bottle can meet a brief need without waiting for a distant tap.
>
> **How it maps:** A local capacitor supplies a chip’s brief current demand through a short path, while the supply replenishes it.
>
> **Where it stops:** Capacitance, resistance and inductance determine the electrical response. A larger distant capacitor cannot automatically replace the required local layout.

## Key takeaways

- A local capacitor shortens the path for switching current pulses.
- Use the exact chip and regulator’s specified values and layout.

## Further reading

- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)
- [Analog Devices MT-101: decoupling techniques](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-101.pdf)

questions.prompt: Where should a 100 nF decoupling capacitor for a logic chip be placed?

options.text: As close as possible to the chip's supply pin, with a short path to ground
options.explanation: Correct. TI's datasheet recommends placing the bypass capacitor "as close to the power terminal as possible". Long leads add inductance that defeats the purpose.

options.text: Anywhere on the board's power rail, since it's all connected
options.explanation: Electrically connected, but wire length adds inductance. A distant capacitor can't supply the chip's fast current pulses.

options.text: At the USB connector where power enters
options.explanation: That's where bulk capacitance goes. Decoupling for fast pulses needs to be local to each chip.

options.text: In series with the chip's supply pin
options.explanation: A capacitor in series would block DC and the chip wouldn't power up. Decoupling goes from the supply pin to ground, in parallel with the chip.

questions.workedExample:
1. The chip draws short, fast pulses of current when it switches.
2. The supply wiring's inductance resists fast changes, so the voltage at the pin dips.
3. A capacitor right at the pin supplies the pulse locally.
4. Its effectiveness depends on short connections. Place it next to the chip's supply pin (V_CC), connected from that pin to GND.

questions.prompt: Which statements about decoupling are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chips draw current in fast pulses, and supply wiring can't respond instantly because of its inductance and resistance
options.explanation: Correct. That's why local capacitance is needed.

options.text: A 100 nF capacitor right at the supply pin acts as a local reservoir for those pulses
options.explanation: Correct. TI recommends 0.1 µF for the SN74HC00, placed as close to the power terminal as possible.

options.text: One large capacitor at the power input replaces all local decoupling
options.explanation: A distant capacitor sits behind the same wiring inductance. Bulk capacitance complements local decoupling but doesn't replace it.

options.text: Supply noise from digital switching can reach audio circuits sharing the supply
options.explanation: Correct. The same rail feeds the audio parts, so digital switching noise can become audible. The noise units develop this.

questions.workedExample:
1. Fast switching current pulses + inductive supply path = local voltage dips.
2. A local 100 nF ceramic supplies the high-frequency part of the current.
3. Bulk electrolytics at the power entry handle slower, larger changes. Both are needed.
4. Any noise left on the rail is shared by everything on it, including codecs and op-amps.

lessons.title: Reading schematic symbols and nets
lessons.summary: Follow nets, pin numbers, labels and junctions rather than page geometry.
lessons.body:
A schematic says *what connects to what*. A breadboard is one physical way to make those connections. The skill is moving between the two without error, and checking your work before power goes on.

## Common symbols
Symbols vary between the US/ANSI style and the IEC style used in Europe. You'll meet both.

| Part | Symbol notes | Designator |
|---|---|---|
| Resistor | Zigzag (US) or rectangle (IEC) | R1, R2 |
| Capacitor | Two parallel plates | C1 |
| Polarised capacitor | One plate curved or marked + | C2 |
| Diode | Diode symbol with a cathode bar; not a current arrow | D1 |
| LED | Diode with outward arrows | D2, LED1 |
| Potentiometer | Resistor with an arrow (wiper) | RV1, VR1 |
| Switch / button | Broken line with a lever | SW1, S1 |
| IC | Box with numbered pins | U1, IC1 |
| Connector / jack | Varies; pins numbered | J1, P1 |
| Ground | Downward lines or a triangle | GND |
| Supply | Arrow, bar or label (+5V, 3V3) | VCC |

The **reference designator** (R1, C3, U2) links each symbol to the parts list and to the board's silkscreen. Use designators in your notes too: "R3 is wrong" is unambiguous.

## Reading a schematic
### Nets, not pictures

A schematic is a graph made of schematic nets. Each **net** is a set of pins joined together electrically. Wire lengths and positions mean nothing; only connections do.

- **Junction dots** mark wires that connect. Two wires crossing *without* a dot don't connect. Many drawing conventions avoid four-way junctions entirely, so a cross is never ambiguous.
- **Net labels:** two wires with the same label (for example `ADC0` or `+3V3`) are connected even if no line joins them.
- **Power and ground symbols** are net labels too. Matching symbols for the same named ground or supply identify that net within the schematic’s scope. Distinct AGND and DGND symbols or hierarchical labels need the design’s own connection rules.
- **Hidden power pins:** some schematics omit an IC's supply pins from the drawing. Check the datasheet pinout so you don't forget to power the chip.

### Conventions that help

- Signals usually flow **left to right**: inputs on the left, outputs on the right.
- Higher voltages at the **top**, ground at the **bottom**.
- Values sit beside designators: `R1 10k`, `C4 100n`.

> [!example] Reading a pot input
> `+3V3 → RV1 pin 3`, `RV1 pin 1 → GND`, `RV1 pin 2 → net ADC0`, `C5 100n from ADC0 to GND`, and elsewhere `ADC0 → U1 pin 14`. That's three nets: +3V3, GND and ADC0. ADC0 has three members: the pot’s wiper, one terminal of the capacitor and U1 pin 14.

## Key takeaways

- Follow nets, pin numbers, labels and junctions rather than page geometry.
- Reference designators identify actual parts.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: reading schematics](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-read-a-schematic/all)
- [TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/sn74hc00.pdf)

questions.prompt: On a schematic, two wires cross with no dot where they meet. Are they connected?

options.text: Yes, all crossing wires connect
options.explanation: Crossing without a junction dot means no connection. Dots mark joins.

options.text: Only if they carry the same voltage
options.explanation: Connection is shown by the drawing, not inferred from voltages.

options.text: Only if they're the same colour
options.explanation: Schematic line colour has no electrical meaning.

options.text: No. A junction dot marks a connection; a plain crossing isn't one
options.explanation: Correct. That's the standard convention, which is why careful schematics also avoid four-way junctions.

questions.workedExample:
1. Look for a filled dot at the crossing.
2. No dot means the wires pass over each other without connecting.
3. A dot means they join into one net.
4. Net labels are the other way to join wires: same label, same net.

questions.prompt: A repair note says “check U3”. On this schematic, U designators identify integrated circuits. How do you locate the intended part?

options.text: Choose any resistor near the fault
options.explanation: Physical proximity does not identify the reference designator.

options.text: Look for the third connector in the wiring order
options.explanation: The number is an identifier, not the order in which wires must be connected.

options.text: Match U3 on the schematic to U3 in the parts list and board markings
options.explanation: Correct. A reference designator ties the circuit drawing to a particular physical part.

options.text: Treat U3 as a voltage measurement of three volts
options.explanation: A reference designator is a part label, not a voltage value.

questions.workedExample: Use the designator consistently across drawing, parts list and physical layout. The prefix convention identifies the part class here, while the complete label identifies the specific instance. Check the exact part number and pinout before testing or replacing it.

questions.prompt: A schematic shows a net labelled `ADC0` at the pot's wiper, and a separate wire labelled `ADC0` on pin 14 of U1, with no line between them. What should you wire?

options.text: Connect the pot's wiper to U1 pin 14
options.explanation: Correct. Identical net labels belong to the same net, so they must be electrically joined.

options.text: Nothing: unconnected lines mean no connection
options.explanation: Same-named net labels are connected by definition. That's how schematics avoid long wires.

options.text: Connect the wiper to ground
options.explanation: The label is ADC0, not GND. Ground is a separate net.

options.text: Connect them only if a junction dot is shown
options.explanation: Junction dots matter for wires that cross. Net labels connect by name.

questions.workedExample:
1. Net labels join everything with the same name.
2. Two `ADC0` labels mean one net: wiper ↔ U1 pin 14.
3. On the breadboard, give ADC0 one strip and run a jumper from the wiper to it and from it to the board pin.
4. Add `ADC0` to your connection table.

lessons.title: Breadboard connections and net-by-net wiring
lessons.summary: Verify the board’s internal strips and any split rails unpowered.
lessons.body:
Verify the board’s internal strips and any split rails unpowered.

## How a breadboard is connected
A solderless breadboard has spring clips under the holes, joined in fixed groups:

```diagram
  + rail  ● ● ● ● ●   ● ● ● ● ●
  − rail  ● ● ● ● ●   ● ● ● ● ●

 row:  1   2   3   4   5   6
   a   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   b   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   c   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   d   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   e   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
      ===== centre channel =====
   f   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   g   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   h   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   i   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●
   j   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●   ●

  − rail  ● ● ● ● ●   ● ● ● ● ●
  + rail  ● ● ● ● ●   ● ● ● ● ●
```

- **Terminal strips:** in each numbered row, holes a–e are connected to each other, and f–j are connected to each other. The two halves are **not** connected across the centre channel.
- **Centre channel:** DIP chips straddle it, so each pin gets its own strip.
- **Power rails:** long strips along each edge, usually marked red (+) and blue or black (−).
- **Rails on opposite sides aren't connected.** Bridge them with jumpers if you want the same supply on both sides.
- **Some boards split the rails halfway along.** A gap in the red or blue line often marks this. Check with a continuity tester, because a split rail is a classic "half my circuit is dead" bug.

## From schematic to breadboard
A systematic method avoids most wiring errors:

1. **Number the nets.** Write every net from the schematic as a list: GND, +3V3, ADC0, LED_A, and so on.
2. **Give each net a home.** Power and ground go on the rails. Each other net gets one terminal strip (or several joined by a jumper).
3. **Place ICs across the channel first,** with pin 1 in a known row. Then place parts around them.
4. **Plug each component lead into the strip for its net.** A resistor between ADC0 and GND has one lead in the ADC0 row and one on the − rail.
5. **Avoid shorting a component to itself.** Both legs of a resistor in the same strip bypass its resistance: both ends are on the same net.
6. **Colour code wires:** red for positive supply, black or blue for ground, other colours for signals. It's a convention, not a rule, but it makes checking much faster.
7. **Tick off each connection** on the schematic as you make it.

> [!tip] Breadboard limits
> Breadboards are for low-voltage, low-current, low-frequency prototyping. Spring contacts have some resistance and can loosen. Adjacent strips add stray capacitance whose value depends on the board and wiring. Long jumpers pick up noise. An audio prototype can be noisier than a well laid out finished board. Record the limitation and investigate unexplained hum rather than assuming every noise is unavoidable.

## Key takeaways

- Verify the board’s internal strips and any split rails unpowered.
- Place component ends on the intended different nets.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: breadboard connections](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-breadboard/all)
- [SparkFun: reading schematics](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-read-a-schematic/all)

questions.prompt: On a standard breadboard, which holes are connected to hole 12a?

options.text: 12b, 12c, 12d and 12e
options.explanation: Correct. In each numbered row, a–e form one strip. f–j form a separate strip on the other side of the channel.

options.text: 12b to 12j
options.explanation: The centre channel separates a–e from f–j. They aren't connected.

options.text: 11a and 13a
options.explanation: Neighbouring rows are separate strips. Connection runs across a row, not along the column.

options.text: Every hole in column a
options.explanation: Column a is a set of separate strips, one per row. Only the power rails run the board's length.

questions.workedExample:
1. A terminal strip is a 5-hole spring clip under a–e (or f–j) of one row.
2. 12a shares a clip with 12b, 12c, 12d, 12e.
3. 12f–12j are a different clip across the channel.
4. Row 11 and row 13 are separate clips.

questions.prompt: You put a resistor on the breadboard with one leg in 20c and the other in 20e. The circuit doesn't work. Why?

options.text: The resistor is the wrong value
options.explanation: The value is not the fault here: the strip directly joins both resistor ends, bypassing the resistor’s intended resistance between different nets.

options.text: Both legs are in the same strip, so the resistor is shorted out and does nothing
options.explanation: Correct. 20a–20e are one node, so both ends sit on the same net. Place the legs in different rows.

options.text: Resistors must straddle the centre channel
options.explanation: Only DIP ICs need to straddle the channel. Resistors can go anywhere their legs land in different nets.

options.text: The resistor is in backwards
options.explanation: Resistors aren't polarised.

questions.workedExample:
1. 20c and 20e share the a–e clip in row 20.
2. Both resistor ends are therefore on the same net, with no voltage across them and no current through them.
3. Move one leg to another row, say 24c, so the resistor connects the net in row 20 to the net in row 24.

questions.prompt: Half of a long breadboard circuit has no power, although the + rail is fed at one end. The components on the dead half are correctly wired. What should you suspect first?

options.text: A failed resistor
options.explanation: One failed resistor wouldn't remove power from everything on that half.

options.text: The supply is too weak
options.explanation: A weak supply would affect both halves, not cleanly cut off one.

options.text: The rails are split halfway along the board, so the far half isn't connected
options.explanation: Correct. Many full-size breadboards split their power rails in the middle. Check with continuity and bridge the gap with jumpers.

options.text: The centre channel blocks the rail
options.explanation: The centre channel separates the a–e and f–j strips. It doesn't run across the rails.

questions.workedExample:
1. The symptom is a clean cut between working and dead parts along the rail.
2. Many breadboards split each rail into two halves. A break in the printed red or blue line is a common hint.
3. Confirm with power off: meter in continuity mode between the rail's two ends.
4. Fix: add a short jumper across the gap on each split rail.

questions.prompt: A DIP-14 chip is placed on a breadboard with all its pins in row-strips a–e only, not straddling the channel. What's wrong?

options.text: Nothing, as long as it's pushed in firmly
options.explanation: Each strip joins five holes. Pins in the same row would be shorted to each other.

options.text: Opposite pins of the chip land in the same strip, shorting them together
options.explanation: Correct. A DIP has two rows of pins. Straddling the channel gives every pin its own strip.

options.text: The chip will be upside down
options.explanation: Orientation is a separate issue (pin 1 marker). The problem here is shorting.

options.text: DIP chips must go on the power rails
options.explanation: Only power connections go to rails. The chip body straddles the centre channel.

questions.workedExample:
1. A DIP package has two parallel rows of pins, 0.3 in (7.62 mm) apart for narrow DIPs.
2. Without straddling, a pin from each side ends up in the same 5-hole strip, so they're shorted.
3. Straddling the channel puts each pin on its own strip (one side on a–e, the other on f–j).
4. Then check pin 1's position before wiring.

lessons.title: Documenting a reproducible prototype
lessons.summary: Keep the schematic, pin table, parts, photos and measurements together.
lessons.body:
Keep the schematic, pin table, parts, photos and measurements together.

## Documenting wiring
Your future self, or the project's success criteria ("wiring, parts, limitations ... documented"), needs enough detail to rebuild the circuit:

- **A schematic** with designators and values. A hand drawing photographed is fine early on.
- **A connection table** for anything wired to a board's pins:

| Net | From | To |
|---|---|---|
| +3V3 | Board 3V3 pin | RV1 pin 3 |
| ADC0 | `RV1 pin 2` | Documented ADC input |
| GND | Board GND | RV1 pin 1, rail − |

- **A photo** of the breadboard, taken from above in good light.
- **The exact parts:** manufacturer part numbers or at least values and types, and the board model and revision.
- **What you measured** (expected against actual) and the date.

Keep it with the code in version control, so a wiring change and the code that expects it stay together.

## Key takeaways

- Keep the schematic, pin table, parts, photos and measurements together.
- Name the exact board revision and documentation checked.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: reading schematics](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-read-a-schematic/all)
- [SparkFun: breadboard connections](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-breadboard/all)

questions.prompt: Which items belong in the documentation of a breadboard prototype that someone else must be able to rebuild? Select all that apply.

options.text: A schematic with reference designators and values
options.explanation: Correct. It defines the circuit independently of the layout.

options.text: A table mapping each net to the board's physical pins
options.explanation: Correct. Board pins are the commonest source of errors, and a table makes them explicit.

options.text: The board's exact model and revision, and the part numbers used
options.explanation: Correct. Pinouts and voltage limits change between revisions, so record what you used and when.

options.text: Only a photo of the breadboard
options.explanation: A photo helps but hides connections under parts and wires. On its own it isn't enough to rebuild from.

questions.workedExample:
1. The schematic carries intent: nets, values, designators.
2. The connection table carries the mapping to physical pins.
3. Model, revision and part numbers pin down the facts that change between versions.
4. A photo is a useful extra but ambiguous on its own.
5. Add measurements (expected against actual) and the date. Keep it all in version control.

lessons.title: Checking a prototype before first power
lessons.summary: Check component polarity, rail resistance and supply voltage before power.
lessons.body:
Check component polarity, rail resistance and supply voltage before power.

## Before you apply power
Do these checks every time, and they become fast:

1. **Visual check:** every polarised part (electrolytics, diodes, LEDs, ICs) the right way round. No stray wire ends or component legs touching.
2. **Supply to ground, power off:** use the meter's resistance or continuity mode across the supply rails. A steady near-zero reading or unexplained continuous beep means stop and investigate. Continuity thresholds vary: a beep alone does not prove a dead short. A brief beep that stops can be capacitors charging from the meter. Remove all power sources and discharge stored energy before this test.
3. **Check rail continuity:** each rail connects end to end (or you know where it's split).
4. **Check the supply's voltage before connecting it:** measure the supply's output on its own.
5. **Limit the current if you can:** a bench supply with an adjustable current limit, set just above the expected draw, can reduce sustained fault current. It cannot guarantee protection: supply output capacitance, current-limit reaction delay, device limits and wiring still matter.
6. **First power-up:** observe the supply current and watch for abnormal heat or smell; use a suitable thermometer if needed. Do not touch exposed energised conductors or hot components. Anything getting hot or smelling means disconnect at once.
7. **Measure the rails powered:** confirm the supply voltage at the chip's pins, not just at the supply.

```flow
Visual check of polarity and stray leads
Unpowered resistance check across rails
Verify supply voltage on its own
Set current limit if available
Power up and watch for heat or smell
Measure rail voltages at the chips
```

## Key takeaways

- Check component polarity, rail resistance and supply voltage before power.
- A current limit reduces available fault current but cannot guarantee protection.

## Further reading

- [Keysight E3633A/E3634A: load and output-capacitance limits](https://www.keysight.com/us/en/assets/9018-01164/user-manuals/9018-01164.pdf)
- [Tektronix: bench-supply CV/CC operation](https://www.tek.com/en/blog/bench-power-supply-basics)
- [SparkFun: breadboard connections](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-breadboard/all)
- [Fluke: resistance measurement](https://www.fluke.com/en-us/learn/blog/digital-multimeters/how-to-measure-resistance)
- [SparkFun: using a multimeter](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-multimeter/all)

questions.prompt: Before first power-up, you measure resistance between the + and − rails with the circuit unpowered. The meter beeps briefly, then shows a rising and eventually high resistance. What does this suggest?

options.text: A dead short: stop and find it
options.explanation: A steady unexpectedly low resistance warrants investigation. The rising reading here is instead consistent with capacitor charging, though it does not prove the circuit is fault-free.

options.text: The meter is faulty
options.explanation: This is expected behaviour with capacitors across the rails.

options.text: The rails are split
options.explanation: Split rails would show open circuit along the rail, not a brief beep across + and −.

options.text: The meter may be charging capacitors; this does not by itself prove the circuit is ready for power
options.explanation: Correct. A rising reading is consistent with capacitor charging, but complete the other checks before applying power.

questions.workedExample: A resistance meter applies a small test stimulus. Discharged capacitors can initially draw current and then draw less as they charge, giving a rising reading. This is consistent with capacitance, not a complete safety verdict. Investigate any unexplained steady low reading, check the meter’s continuity threshold and complete the polarity, supply and wiring checks before power-up.

questions.prompt: You have a bench supply with an adjustable current limit. Your prototype should draw about 40 mA. How should you set it for first power-up, and why?

options.text: Maximum, so the circuit never starves
options.explanation: With the limit at maximum, a short draws all the supply can give, which can damage parts or wiring.

options.text: Use a documented initial limit modestly above expected draw, perhaps 60–80 mA for this illustrative circuit, and check startup and component limits
options.explanation: Correct. Limiting sustained fault current can help reveal a problem, but the supply’s current-limit reaction delay and stored energy mean it cannot guarantee that every component survives a short.

options.text: Exactly 40 mA
options.explanation: Startup surges and normal variation could trip the limit and confuse you. Leave some margin.

options.text: The current limit doesn't matter at low voltage
options.explanation: Low voltage limits shock risk, but a short at low voltage can still pass enough current to overheat parts and wiring.

questions.workedExample:
1. Estimate the normal draw: 40 mA.
2. Choose a documented initial limit allowing expected startup while respecting component and supply limits.
3. Power up and watch the supply's current reading and limit indicator.
4. If it hits the limit, the voltage collapses instead of the current rising. Switch off and find the fault.
5. Once the circuit is verified, raise the limit to suit the real load.

The 60–80 mA range is an illustrative starting point, not a universal safe limit. Check inrush, supply output capacitance and the smallest allowed current or energy in the real circuit.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in the pre-power checklist? Select all that apply.

options.text: Measure resistance across a component while the circuit is powered, to confirm its value
options.explanation: Resistance must be measured unpowered. Powered, the reading is wrong and the meter can be damaged.

options.text: Check every polarised part's orientation against the schematic
options.explanation: Correct. Reversed electrolytics, diodes and ICs are among the commonest fatal mistakes.

options.text: Measure resistance between the supply rails with power off
options.explanation: Correct. It helps find unexpectedly low-resistance paths before normal supply power is applied; the meter itself uses a small test stimulus.

options.text: Measure the supply's output voltage on its own before connecting it
options.explanation: Correct. It confirms you're about to apply the voltage you think you are.

questions.workedExample:
Pre-power checklist:

1. Visual: component polarity, stray leads.
2. Unpowered: resistance or continuity across the rails. An unexplained steady near-zero reading needs investigation; a beep alone depends on the meter threshold.
3. Supply: measure its voltage before connecting.
4. Current limit set, if available.
5. Power up, watch for heat or smell, then measure rails at the chips.

Resistance measurements are always made with the power off. The measurement units explain why.

lessons.title: Voltage measurement, ranges and meter loading
lessons.summary: Voltage is measured across two points with the correct jack and range.
lessons.body:
Measuring tells you whether the circuit is doing what you calculated. Soldering makes a circuit permanent. Both are hands-on skills with a few rules that, if you ignore them, destroy fuses, parts or your lungs.

> [!warning] Low-voltage work only
> Everything here assumes low-voltage DC circuits powered from USB, batteries or a bench supply. Don't use these techniques on mains-powered equipment. Mains measurement needs suitably rated (CAT-rated) instruments and training, and it's outside this project's scope.

## Meter inputs
A digital multimeter (DMM) has a rotary switch and usually three or four input jacks:

- **COM:** the common (black) lead. It stays here for everything.
- **VΩ** (shared with current only on some meters): red lead for voltage, resistance, continuity and diode test.
- **mA / µA:** red lead for small currents, protected by a fuse.
- **A or 10A:** red lead for large currents, fused only if the meter’s manual specifies it; some inexpensive meters leave that input unfused.

The jack layout differs between meters, so read the manual.

## Voltage: in parallel
Put the probes **across** the thing you're measuring, black on the reference (usually ground) and red on the point of interest. Nothing gets disconnected.

```diagram
  +5V ──[ R1 ]──┬──[ LED ]── GND
                │
             red probe
   (black probe on GND)
```

- Use **DC volts** (V⎓) for supply rails and logic. AC volts usually rejects the DC component, so it will not tell you a rail’s steady voltage. An average-responding meter is RMS-calibrated for a sine wave; other waveforms need a suitable true-RMS instrument within its frequency, crest-factor and range limits.
- A digital meter's voltage input is high-impedance, typically around 10 MΩ on DC volts, though some meters and ranges differ (check your meter's specification). It barely loads most circuits, but on a very high-resistance divider the meter itself pulls the reading down. The divider-loading lesson's rule applies to meters too.
- A negative DC reading means the red probe is below the black probe in voltage. The probes may be reversed, or the measured voltage may genuinely have the opposite polarity.

## Choosing ranges
Autoranging meters choose for you. On a manual meter:

- **Start on a range above the largest value you expect,** then step down for resolution.
- An "OL" or "1" display indicates a meter over-range. Go up a range.
- For current, start on the highest range if you're unsure, which on many meters means moving the red lead to the A jack.

## Key takeaways

- Voltage is measured across two points with the correct jack and range.
- The meter’s finite input impedance can load high-resistance circuits.

## Further reading

- [SparkFun: using a multimeter](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/how-to-use-a-multimeter/all)
- [SparkFun: voltage dividers](https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/voltage-dividers/all)

questions.prompt: How do you connect a multimeter to measure the voltage on an LED's anode?

options.text: In series: break the wire to the anode and connect the meter across the gap
options.explanation: That's how you measure current. Voltage is measured across two points without breaking anything.

options.text: In parallel: black probe on ground, red probe on the anode, meter set to DC volts
options.explanation: Correct. A voltage is a difference between two points, so the probes go across them. Nothing is disconnected.

options.text: In parallel, with the red lead in the mA jack
options.explanation: In the mA jack the meter is nearly a short. Connected across a voltage it shorts the circuit and blows the fuse.

options.text: Either way, as long as the meter is on autorange
options.explanation: Autorange picks the scale, not the connection method. Voltage is always measured in parallel.

questions.workedExample:
1. Voltage is between two points: here, anode and ground.
2. Red lead in VΩ, black in COM, switch to DC volts.
3. Black probe to ground, red probe to the anode.
4. Read. A negative sign means the red probe is below the black probe in voltage; the probes may be reversed or the polarity may genuinely be opposite.

questions.prompt: A divider of two 10 MΩ resistors across 3.3 V should give 1.65 V. Your DMM, with a 10 MΩ input impedance, reads about 1.1 V. Why?

options.text: The meter's 10 MΩ input is in parallel with the bottom 10 MΩ, making it 5 MΩ, so the divider gives 3.3 V × 5/15 = 1.1 V
options.explanation: Correct. A meter is a load like any other. Here it's as large as the divider's own resistors.

options.text: The meter is broken
options.explanation: The meter is behaving correctly. It's loading the circuit.

options.text: Voltage must be measured in series
options.explanation: Voltage is measured in parallel. The issue is the meter's finite input resistance.

options.text: 10 MΩ resistors are too noisy to measure
options.explanation: Noise isn't the cause of a steady, predictable 1.1 V reading.

questions.workedExample: The meter is connected across the lower divider resistor, so its finite input resistance becomes a parallel branch. Here the meter and lower resistor have equal resistance, making the effective lower resistance smaller and pulling the voltage down. The displayed 1.1 V is therefore consistent with loading rather than proof of a faulty meter. Use a suitably buffered or higher-impedance measurement, or account for the load in the design.

questions.prompt: On a manual-ranging meter, you need to measure a voltage you expect to be about 3.3 V. The ranges are 200 mV, 2 V, 20 V and 200 V. Which do you choose?

options.text: 200 mV, for the most precision
options.explanation: 3.3 V is far above 200 mV, so the display indicates a meter over-range (OL or 1).

options.text: 2 V
options.explanation: 3.3 V exceeds the 2 V range limit, so the display indicates a meter over-range.
Correct. It's the lowest range above the anticipated reading, giving the best resolution without meter over-range.

options.text: 200 V, to be safe
options.explanation: It works but wastes resolution: you'd see 3 V or 3.3 V rather than 3.30 V.

questions.workedExample:
1. Choose the lowest range that's still above the anticipated reading.
2. 3.3 V > 2 V, so the 2 V and 200 mV ranges both give a meter over-range.
3. 20 V gives readings like 3.30 V.
4. If you don't know the value at all, start at the highest range and step down.

lessons.title: Measuring series current and burden voltage
lessons.summary: Power off before inserting the meter in series.
lessons.body:
Power off before inserting the meter in series.

## Current: in series
To measure current, the current has to flow **through** the meter. Break the circuit and insert the meter into the gap:

```diagram
  +5V ──[ R1 ]──  ✂  ──[ LED ]── GND
              red    black
               └─ meter ─┘
```

1. Power off.
2. Move the red lead to the **mA** jack (or the A jack for larger currents) and select the current range.
3. Open the circuit at one point and connect the meter across the gap.
4. Power on and read.
5. **Power off and move the red lead back to VΩ** before your next measurement.

> [!warning] The classic fuse-blower
> In current mode the meter is almost a short circuit, by design. Put it *across* a supply (as you would for voltage) and you short the supply through the meter. The meter's fuse is there to blow in that case. Replace it only with the **exact type and rating** the manual specifies. Forgetting to move the red lead back to VΩ is the commonest way to do this.

Meters also have a **burden voltage**: the small voltage the meter drops while measuring current. It comes from the series resistance of the shunt and other current-path parts, including the fuse and connections. Model their combined resistance to estimate it with Ohm’s law.

For an illustrative meter path of 10 Ω carrying 10 mA, the drop is 0.1 V. Check the meter’s specified burden on the selected range and include lead resistance. More sensitive current ranges can impose more burden, so a finer display is not always a less disturbing measurement.
